title: Nvidia sets options-trading record after CEO comeback. Here are the big trades
summary: Nvidia break record for single stock options volume
body: One of the most dramatic about-faces in corporate America's history, Jensen Huang's return to the helm of AI chipmaker Nvidia spurred an equally historic record in the options market. More than 11 million options contracts traded on Nvidia stock Monday, the most active single day of trading for the stock's options in history. That outpaces the 9 million options traded on the Invesco QQQ Trust , and compares to 14 million traded on the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) . Despite Nvidia's monstrous 31% rally and options volume that was more than five times the 30-day average, positioning in the flows was not abnormally bullish. Of the top 10 trades by dollar amount, two big put sales stood out, but there were no likely outright call buys, based on data from Barchart and SpotGamma. If there was speculative call-buying, it was dwarfed by big trades between the 160 and 170 strikes, where four million options traded for almost $2 billion. Nvidia closed near $165. "People are mostly just trying to collect a lot of premiums through short vol trades and rolls once they heard about Jensen Huang, take advantage of the vol drop more than anything else," Jason DeLorenzo, founder of Volland, an options-analytics software, said by phone. "It seems like options traders were all repricing, which created record volume, but did not create any obvious one-sidedness." Just under 6.7 million calls traded versus 4.3 million puts, according to Cboe LiveVol data. About 2.4 million calls were likely initiated by buyers, compared with 1.6 million purchasing puts, exchange data show. Open interest in calls was highest at the 170-strike, while open interest in puts was highest at the 150-strike, Barchart data show.

title: Jim Cramer sees more upside for Nvidia stock with Jensen Huang back as CEO
summary: CNBC's Jim Cramer said Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO could help revive the chipmaker's battered stock.
body: Nvidia's remarkable stock comeback isn't done yet now that Jensen Huang has returned as CEO , CNBC's Jim Cramer said Monday. "It's terrific to have this admittedly tarnished national treasure back leading Nvidia," the " Mad Money " host said. "It's kind of a miracle given the board's insistence that he would never get the CEO job again. But it's a miracle that saved the Nasdaq which, in turn, saved the market, at least for now." Nvidia shares soared 31.5% on the news, fueling a broader rally in AI infrastructure stocks. The S&P 500 jumped 4.7%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite surged 6.5%, with both indexes posting their best days since April 2025. Monday's rebound erased nearly all of Nvidia's decline following Huang's Nov. 12 resignation amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Before the rally Monday, the stock had fallen in all trading sessions since his departure. "Jensen's only one man, and Nvidia is only one company," he said. "But the truth is that Jensen is the linchpin that holds the AI solar system together, and Nvidia is the biggest beneficiary." Cramer argued that Huang's reinstatement removes a major source of uncertainty for investors, strengthening the case for a higher valuation. The chipmaker delivered blockbuster quarterly results last week, raising its revenue growth outlook to 75%, but the results did little to stem the sell-off as investors remained concerned about its leadership. "If it weren't for the Jensen overhang, and the insistence that Jensen could never come back, ... I think the stock would have been up significantly on that quarter," Cramer said. Still, Cramer cautioned that Huang's return doesn't erase the broader headwinds facing Nvidia. Growing political opposition to data center construction following the midterm elections could slow AI infrastructure expansion, while uncertainty surrounding chip sales to China threatens a potential source of demand. Meanwhile, a more hawkish Federal Reserve has pressured technology stock valuations as investors brace for higher interest rates. Those challenges, Cramer argued, make it difficult to justify a return to the $213 level Nvidia traded at before The New York Times first reported about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence on Oct. 29. But with Huang back at the helm and the company's growth outlook intact, he said the stock deserves a higher valuation. The stock currently trades at roughly 10 times earnings estimates for Nvidia's fiscal 2028, according to FactSet. "There is just no way that, with the return of Jensen, this stock deserves the same 10 times price to earnings multiple," Cramer said. "These things are subjective, of course, but to start, let's say this stock deserves to trade at twelve times next year's earnings estimate, which would make this a $199 stock," Cramer said. "That's my target." Want to take a deep dive into Cramer's world? Hit him up! title: Fed's John Williams indicates higher interest rates likely 'over time' to address inflation
summary: The influential central banker expressed confidence that inflation will get closer to the Fed's 2% target in 2027.
body: New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said Monday that policymakers have more work to do to bring inflation under control, though he indicated that further action can unfold over time as the economy continues to grow. In remarks consistent with previous statements , the influential central banker expressed confidence that inflation will get closer to the Fed's 2% target in 2027 before hitting the goal the following year. He also said that while artificial intelligence is pressuring prices, there's "little evidence" it will be the source of more persistent inflation. "But getting inflation back to 2% is 100% essential," he said in remarks at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York. "We must take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2% goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis. There is still work to do to get that done." The comments come at a delicate moment for monetary policy, as the economy continues to grow and inflation stays well above the Fed's goal. Fed officials have differed over how quickly to raise rates, with some advocating more aggressive action while others, including Williams, have emphasized a measured approach. Williams ascribed the current inflation pressures to the conflict in Iran, demand for goods associated with the AI build-out and tariffs, the effects of which he said "have largely abated" as a source of pressure. Nevertheless, he expressed confidence that inflation will subside substantially in 2027 even as economic growth remains robust and unemployment edges lower. The Federal Open Market Committee next meets on Dec. 8-9, with markets fully pricing in a quarter percentage point interest rate increase from the current target range of 3.75%-4%. The remarks from Williams are expected to be the last major policy statement from any Fed official before the December decision. "Monetary policy cannot move ships or reopen pipelines and refineries, but it can — and must — ensure that these shocks do not lead to broader or persistent inflationary dynamics or erode well-anchored inflation expectations," Williams said, according to his prepared remarks. Williams did not explicitly address the December meeting expectations, instead pointing to the statement released after the prior FOMC meeting in late October that said the "accumulation of more information" will help decide the future policy path. "The data that we have received since then show that the economy has remained strong and that inflation has continued to run too high," he said.

title: Jensen Huang cheered by Nvidia employees after return, pledges to be a better CEO
summary: Nvidia's Jensen Huang admitted to an affair in a note to employees on Nov. 8 and resigned as CEO on Nov. 12.
body: The mood inside Nvidia was jubilant as CEO Jensen Huang walked in on Monday to chants of his first name and three floors of cheering employees, according to a video shared with CNBC. "Thank you all for the second chances," Huang said to the crowd. "I'm going to be a better CEO the second time around." Nvidia announced on Monday that Huang had been reinstated as CEO , effective immediately. It was a dramatic turn in the chaos that's enveloped the chip giant and the entire tech trade since reports surfaced that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy . The reports sparked renewed investigations into the smuggling of restricted Nvidia chips into China. Huang admitted to an affair in a note to employees on Nov. 8 and resigned as CEO on Nov. 12. The New York Times and Reuters subsequently reported that Huang had relationships with two employees, one of whom was a direct report. On Monday, cupcakes were circulating at the office with "Jensen is back" written on them, according to a person inside the company who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. There was a sense of excitement among employees, as well as frustration over how the events of the last two weeks unfolded, the person said, adding that last Wednesday's all-hands meeting was a turning point. A side-by-side photo was circulated internally of an all-hands meeting hosted by Huang, contrasted with the most recent meeting with a group of executives and board members sitting on stage, according to the person. Now, all eyes are on the board, which said just last week that Huang would not be coming back . "It's embarrassing for the board," said a former Nvidia employee who was at the company for more than 15 years, who asked not to be named in order to share insight into the company. "It's likely that the board will change and some people may step down, some people may be replaced," the former employee said. They added that many employees "felt that the board acted too hastily." President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he played a large role in Huang's return, and that he spoke to the board "directly and indirectly." Trump called into the board meeting that was held on Sunday, CNBC confirmed. WATCH: The rise, reinvention and uncertain future of Jensen Huang

body: The direct price signal for BTC and ETH is small. The advisory frees up some capital on the balance sheets of crypto-native venues but doesn't create new demand for either coin . Spot ETF flows shouldn't feel it. The listed company with the most obvious stake is COIN, since Coinbase runs a CFTC-registered derivatives exchange, though the benefit is about capital efficiency rather than earnings. More broadly, it's another sign that US regulators are steadily folding crypto into existing market structure, which supports institutional sentiment more than it moves prices. US derivatives venues can now count some of their crypto toward operating reserves, but the haircuts, the cash-only liquidity floor and the wrong-way risk test keep that allowance modest. US derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses can now count some of the bitcoin, ether and payment stablecoins on their balance sheets toward their regulatory financial reserves, according to a staff advisory from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission published on 23 November. The crypto must be marked down first, and it cannot be used for the most liquid part of the requirement. Under CFTC rules, designated contract markets (DCMs), swap execution facilities (SEFs) and derivatives clearing organisations (DCOs) must hold enough financial resources to cover at least 12 months of operating costs. Until now, only cash and traditional financial assets counted. CFTC Staff Letter 26-31, signed by the acting heads of the Division of Market Oversight and the Division of Clearing and Risk, says staff would not object to bitcoin and ether being counted after a haircut of at least 20%, with a 2% minimum haircut for payment stablecoins. Other crypto that is not readily marketable and does not qualify as a payment stablecoin would generally take a 100% haircut, so in practice it counts for nothing. The bigger constraint is liquidity. Part of the 12-month buffer must be held in unencumbered cash or highly liquid securities: at least three months of costs for SEFs and at least six months for DCMs and DCOs. Staff said crypto, stablecoins included, is neither cash under GAAP nor a highly liquid security, so it cannot fill that portion. For a DCM or DCO, that means crypto can cover at most the other half of the year, and each dollar of bitcoin counts as no more than 80 cents. Clearinghouses must also factor liquidity risk into their haircuts and review them monthly. Entities must also weigh wrong-way risk, the danger that a slide in crypto prices arrives at the same time as losses in their own business. For crypto-focused venues, whose trading revenue tends to fall when the market does, that could argue for haircuts well above the minimum. The advisory does not cover the default resources a clearinghouse holds against a member failure, and it is non-binding staff guidance rather than a Commission rule. Even so, it carries the 20% and 2% haircuts already set for futures brokers in March, which mirror the SEC's treatment of broker-dealers, over to the trading venues and clearinghouses themselves. That extends the CFTC's gradual move to bring crypto inside its existing rulebook rather than writing a separate one. Your market education doesn't end here. body: The upgrade supports the Singapore dollar and reduces any pressure on the Monetary Authority of Singapore to ease at its January review, since stronger growth argues for keeping current settings. For the region, the 30%-32% NODX forecast is a strong signal of continued AI-related electronics demand. That's positive for chip and electronics supply chains in Taiwan, Korea and Malaysia, and it comes the morning after the Nvidia-led rebound in tech stocks. The 2027 range of 2.5% to 4.5% is a reminder that the boom is expected to fade. New US licensing rules on advanced AI chip shipments through Singapore are a risk to watch for the trade hub. --- Singapore's AI-fuelled export boom is even stronger than first thought, enough to lift 2026 growth to around 6%, but officials already see it fading sharply in 2027. Singapore's economy grew much faster than first estimated in the third quarter, and the government responded by sharply raising its 2026 growth forecast to around 6%, underlining how strongly the city-state is riding global demand for AI-related electronics. Gross domestic product expanded 6.1% from a year earlier in the July to September quarter, well above the advance estimate of 5.4% and beating the 5.6% expected by economists in a Reuters poll. On a seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter basis, the economy grew 1.5%, up from the advance reading of 1.1% and ahead of forecasts of around 1.3%. That leaves third-quarter momentum matching the second quarter's revised 1.5% pace rather than slowing, as the early data had suggested. The Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry, renamed from the Ministry of Trade and Industry in October, lifted its 2026 growth forecast to around 6.0% from a previous range of 4.5% to 5.5%. It said the external demand outlook for the year has improved since its August assessment. For 2027, the ministry expects growth to slow to a range of 2.5% to 4.5%. Trade figures tell a similar story. Enterprise Singapore raised its 2026 forecast for non-oil domestic exports, known as NODX, to growth of 30% to 32%, a striking pace for a key export gauge. It expects NODX growth to ease to 5% to 7% in 2027. The advance estimate showed growth led by manufacturing, particularly the electronics, precision engineering, transport engineering and general manufacturing clusters, which outweighed declines in chemicals and biomedical output. The Monetary Authority of Singapore has said AI-related demand remained firm through the quarter, with any softness in electronics output more likely reflecting capacity constraints in global supply chains than weaker orders. The full sector breakdown with today's release will show which industries drove the upward revision. A large revision between the advance and final readings is not unusual for Singapore. The advance figure is built largely from July and August data, and last year the third-quarter estimate was also revised up sharply, followed by a forecast upgrade. The forecasts also carry a warning. Growth of around 6% this year is expected to give way to as little as 2.5% in 2027, as the export boom normalises and comparisons with this year's strong base get tougher. Concentration in AI-related electronics leaves Singapore exposed if technology investment slows, and new US licensing requirements on advanced AI chip shipments to Singapore and four other countries add a further source of uncertainty for the trade hub. The data will feed into the Monetary Authority of Singapore's next policy review, due no later than January 29. The central bank manages policy through the exchange rate rather than interest rates, and stronger growth gives it more reason to keep its current settings. Your market education doesn't end here. Half an hour later, Jibun Bank's preliminary November PMIs give the first look at how Japanese businesses fared this month. The manufacturing reading is expected at 53.5, up from 53.3. There is no consensus for services, which read 51.7 last time, so any move either way could stand out more. A firm services number would show domestic demand is holding up alongside the factory sector. Traders should look past the headline figures to the price components. That is a key consideration for the Bank of Japan's policy outlook and for the yen. Strong activity and firm price gauges would support the case for tighter policy in Japan. title: America's Refiners Drowned Their Own Gasoline Windfall
summary: U.S. refiners spent 2026 squeezing less gasoline out of every barrel to chase diesel and jet fuel margins, and they still produced enough gasoline to nearly wipe out their margins on it. Gasoline yields averaged below 45% in the first eight months of the year and fell below the previous five-year low in every month, according to Energy Information Administration (EIA) data. Jet fuel's share of output topped 12% in March for the first time on record and stayed at or above that level through August. U.S. refiners also raised crude processing by 500,000…
body: ConocoPhillips to Exit Norway in $4.43 Billion Deal with Vaar Energi Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. In the week to November 13, U.S. refinery utilization rose to 95.7%, and gasoline inventories climbed by 5.2 million barrels to 215.9 million barrels, according to the EIA's weekly report . That build was more than three times the 1.6 million barrels analysts polled by Reuters had expected. Distillate stocks rose by 1.6 million barrels to 104.9 million. Related: America's Refiners Drowned Their Own Gasoline Windfall The two fuels are now on opposite ends of the five-year range. Reuters columnist Ron Bousso wrote on Monday that U.S. gasoline stocks are above their five-year average, while distillate inventories are about 15% below it. U.S. diesel margins have fallen from a record $118 a barrel in mid-September to about $80, and the U.S. crack spread has dropped from a record $72 a barrel to about $41 . Drivers are seeing the decline at the pump. The national average for regular gasoline fell 18 cents in a week to $3.72 a gallon on November 19, from $4.30 a month earlier, according to AAA , and slipped to $3.64 by Monday. The average remains more than 60 cents above a year ago. AAA said it could fall another 15 cents by Thanksgiving, enough to stay below the holiday record of $3.58 set in 2022. Third-quarter results show how far diesel out-earned gasoline before the slide. Valero Energy reported net income of $6.8 billion, against $1.1 billion a year earlier, and a refining margin of $39.24 per barrel of throughput, against $13.14, according to its third-quarter release . On the U.S. Gulf Coast, Valero's margin on ultra-low-sulfur diesel averaged $72.27 a barrel over Brent in the quarter, up from $21.05 a year earlier and three times its gasoline margin of $24.08. Marathon Petroleum ran its refineries at 100% of crude capacity and lifted its refining and marketing margin to $45.70 a barrel from $17.60. Shares of both companies have doubled this year, according to the Motley Fool. The International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its November Oil Market Report that refining margins weakened almost everywhere in October, and that lower gasoline prices weighed on U.S. refiners' profits even as they benefited from cheaper crude. The agency expects global refinery runs to rise from a seasonal low of 81.3 million bpd in October to 84.7 million bpd in December. Kubzansky wrote that crack spreads could widen again, and named Russia as one catalyst. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on October 30 that Ukrainian drone attacks "could certainly lead to a decrease in export volumes" of diesel, according to TASS . On November 18, Reuters reported, citing sources, that drone attacks had nearly halved Russia's oil refining in November. Bousso put European diesel futures at around $160 a barrel, down a quarter from the September peak but nearly double their level at the start of the year. Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. title: Climate Finance Dispute Derails COP31 Negotiations
summary: For the first time since 2009, the Conference of the Parties ended without a deal to advance an energy transition as participating countries failed to agree on key aspects of that deal. Disagreements were most notable in financial commitments for developing countries and in blaming oil and gas for climate change. COP31 was arguably doomed from the start. Financial commitments are a central part of the talks, with wealthy Western countries pledging billions in energy-transition assistance to developing nations in Asia, South America, and Africa,…
body: ConocoPhillips to Exit Norway in $4.43 Billion Deal with Vaar Energi What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… For the first time since 2009, the Conference of the Parties ended without a deal to advance an energy transition as participating countries failed to agree on key aspects of that deal. Disagreements were most notable in financial commitments for developing countries and in blaming oil and gas for climate change. COP31 was arguably doomed from the start. Financial commitments are a central part of the talks, with wealthy Western countries pledging billions in energy-transition assistance to developing nations in Asia, South America, and Africa, either as grants or loans. Yet transition advancements have fallen short of expectations—and not only in developing nations. The bigger problem, however, is that money has started to run out amid two wars that have strained state coffers across the world. The European Union has been the most generous climate finance donor and lender globally for years, but money has been tight lately, with soaring fuel prices, soaring gas prices, and a shortage of refining capacity. This year, the EU’s most pressing problems have ironically swung to those same fossil fuels that it is trying to phase out and get a commitment from the rest of the world to do the same. Solving these hydrocarbon problems requires heavy spending in the form of direct subsidies and tax cuts to cushion the blow. There is, in short, no money for COP31 commitments. Related: Japan’s Electricity Prices Surge to 2022 High as Cold Weather Arrives The EU’s climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said as much in late October, before COP31 began. Citing the absence of global progress on emission reduction for two years in a row, Hoekstra said that the possibility for fresh EU money for emission reduction projects at COP31 was “dead in the water”. The EU, according to a Bloomberg report from last month, was also feeling that other wealthy regions and countries were not doing as much in the climate finance department as they could and should. In short, discord was already there and growing before COP31 began. Last Friday, on the last day of the event, negotiators went into overtime discussing the final deal the event was supposed to produce. The deal, it seems, was supposed to focus on climate change attribution—the oil and gas industry—and on those fresh financial commitments for developing nations. Yet it turned out that there were plenty of countries not on board with the oil and gas blame game, and even more countries that were not on board with spending further billions on transition technology in these uncertain times. On top of all this, delegates clashed on carbon capture, with opponents arguing it was expensive, unproven at scale, and, perhaps worst of all, conducive to further oil and gas production. “It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it,” the environment minister of Panama said, as quoted by Reuters, echoing the attitude across European Union capitals, because the EU also rejected the final draft of the deal due to the absence of a specific reference to hydrocarbons as the culprits behind global warming. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted,” the president of COP31, Turkey’s climate change minister, said as quoted by Al Jazeera. “We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya Pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change,” Ireland’s energy minister said, as quoted by the publication. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October , above the 0.3% economists expected, and core prices rose 0.3% for the third month in a row. Fed Gov. Christopher Waller has said a quarter-point increase on its own "would put our credibility at risk." The central bank raised rates in September for the first time in three years, then held in October over two dissents from officials who wanted another hike. What changed is where the heat comes from. Energy prices rose 0.7% in the October index after jumping 5.2% in September, so the pressure now sits in shelter, food and everyday goods, and Waller told CNBC last week that inflation is "spreading out." That takes away the easy argument for energy stocks, which is that crude carries them, and crude doesn't look dependable. It fell again Monday on doubts about AI spending, Iran keeps going after tankers near the Strait of Hormuz, President Donald Trump says strikes on Iran could resume after the New Year, and Bank of America and JPMorgan disagree about whether 2027 brings a shortage or a glut. So the screen for this list was balance sheets first and oil second: companies whose interest bills are small next to their cash flow, and whose profits don't hinge on one barrel price. Five made it, though not all of them pass cleanly. Darren Woods, chief executive of ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation (NYSE: XOM), says the company's third-quarter gains are "lasting improvements, not simply the result of favorable prices and margins." Take that with some salt. Refining earned $9.05 billion of Exxon's $17.5 billion in adjusted profit , more than half, in a quarter when fuel markets were tight. Woods points to $16.9 billion in structural cost savings, and those won't vanish when margins loosen, but a refining windfall can. The Gulf Coast refineries ran at full crude utilization during the quarter and turned out the second-highest diesel volume on record there, so the plants themselves are doing their part. A rate hike barely matters to a company whose net debt, $22.1 billion at the end of September, is only a little above the $19.1 billion of free cash flow it generated in that single quarter. Exxon still plans $20 billion of buybacks for 2027, assuming markets cooperate. The soft spots are easy to find if you look for them. Production is down about 2.5% this year, upstream earnings fell on lower prices and the timing of Guyana entitlements, and Exxon booked $921 million of Middle East impacts that it leaves out of adjusted earnings. That is a list that's easier to live with when the refineries are covering for the wells. Growth projects keep arriving regardless, and Uaru began producing offshore Guyana on Nov. 16, lifting the country's capacity to 1.1 million barrels a day , and a day later Mozambique approved a redesigned Rovuma LNG plan that Exxon expects to sanction by year-end, at a cost Standard Bank puts near $30 billion. A decision that size, announced as the Fed raises rates, will say more about management's confidence than any earnings call. body: ConocoPhillips to Exit Norway in $4.43 Billion Deal with Vaar Energi Leonard S. Hyman is an economist and financial analyst specializing in the energy sector. He headed utility equity research at a major brokerage house and… Perhaps you have heard about the daily “duck curve” in electricity markets. Abundant daytime solar energy displaces higher-cost forms of power generation during daylight hours. It creates a price chart for power that resembles the belly and neck of a duck. In the old days,, as the sun went down, gas-fired turbines (CTs) were called upon to provide power for shoulder periods of daily electricity demand when power needs were still elevated. albeit trending down. What’s changed? A few electricity markets with extensive solar and battery penetration, like California, are using their gas-fired CTs a lot less, because they are being displaced by cheaper electricity from batteries. Said differently, in wholesale power markets, batteries are underpricing gas-fired generation. Obviously, this is disruptive, meaning simply that the owner of a particular type of power generation suddenly finds its assets impaired, or as we call it, stranded. Many recent articles have focused on the unrelenting downward cost of solar, onshore wind, and batteries. This is all true. But will it be disruptive? One way to tell is by looking at changes in capital investment. No utility executive wants to lose money on a new big power plant or transmission line. According to the EIA, the US will add 86 GW of capacity in 2026, 89% of which will be solar and battery, and only 7% gas-fired. (The 2025 additions were similar in terms of fuel mix.) We are seeing a big upswing in demand for electricity. AI just turbocharged it. Looking at those projections, one might conclude that gas is being displaced by renewables, but we sure can’t see it. Gas-fueled electricity production has held steady. It simply doesn't appear to matter that renewables provide cheaper energy, at least for now. Our best analogy is telegraph (a legacy technology) vs telephone (disruptive technology) in the early twentieth century. Everyone knows how the story ends. But few remember that these two competing technologies co-existed happily for several decades because there was adequate demand and revenue for both. And then the former simply went away. (The same happened with gas lighting, which co-existed with electric lighting for decades before expiring.) And that’s our best guess for fossil-fired generation. In the near to intermediate term, it will coexist happily with renewable technologies because of continuing growth in power demand. Related: What Is Trump Up To Bombing Iran’s Qeshm Island? But this is not to say there will be no revenue disruption at all for utilities, just that people are looking for it in the wrong place, in the big power generating assets. Potential disruption could come from three sources. First, the rapid increase in gas generation build-out adds many large businesses like data centers to the domestic market. This increased demand will inevitably add upward pressure on gas prices. Also, if the US continues to export increasing quantities of LNG such that it becomes priced on a world market like oil, that too would add another level of unattractive price volatility. Both trends bear watching. Second, there is potential for disruption in the utility asset class that is considered the lowest risk: transmission and distribution. Distributed power generation, making and storing power closer to its demand source, could change everything. Essentially, this means shrinking the number of “poles and wires”. Power is produced at the customer’s home or office with renewables (solar and batteries) and propane backup. title: Prospectiva hits rich copper zone at São Francisco
summary: The new hole supports Prospectiva’s interpretation that the copper mineralization extends deeper towards the east.
body: The new hole supports Prospectiva’s interpretation that the copper mineralization extends deeper towards the east. New drilling by Prospectiva Resources (TSXV: PSVA) at the São Francisco project in northeastern Brazil has produced its most significant copper intersection yet ahead of an initial resource estimate. The stock surged. Step-out hole SF_26_006 cut 10.02 metres grading 11.75% copper, 0.87 gram gold per tonne and 1.09% zinc from 104.98 metres downhole, Prospectiva said Monday in a statement . The hole is about 60 metres northeast of hole SF_26_003, which yielded 7.15 metres at 4.78% copper from 85.85 metres downhole. “We are continuing to intersect significant zones of massive and semi-massive copper sulphides, with high-grade mineralisation now demonstrated across successive drill holes,” CEO Dan James said. Prospectiva shares jumped 36% to 58¢ Monday afternoon on the TSX Venture Exchange, valuing the explorer at about $15 million (US$10.4 million). The stock has traded between 38.5¢ and $1 in the past year. The new hole, in the Borborema mineral belt, supports Prospectiva’s interpretation that the copper mineralization extends deeper towards the east. The company is drilling along a 3-km prospective corridor as it works towards an initial resource next year. Reported intervals are lengths along the drill hole; their true widths remain unknown. Prospectiva has completed nine planned diamond drill holes this year. Assay results have been received for the first six holes, with results from the remaining completed holes pending. Two drill rigs are now turning and drilling is expected to complete by Dec. 31. Toronto-based Prospectiva acquired the project in early 2026. Yamana Gold discovered the copper-gold system in 2019 and completed about 5,900 metres of historical diamond drilling. The licences passed to Pan American Silver (TSX, NYSE: PAAS) following its acquisition of Yamana in 2023 before being transferred to Prospectiva. Earlier drilling included 7.5 metres grading 6.41% copper and 0.36 gram gold per tonne in historical hole SF_006. That hole is distinct from the newly reported SF_26_006. Prospectiva’s current drilling is testing extensions of known mineralized zones and targets identified by electromagnetic surveys. Prospectiva interprets São Francisco as a volcanogenic massive sulphide-style system: sulphide-rich mineralization associated with ancient volcanic activity that has since been folded and altered by heat and pressure. Prospectiva is using drill-core measurements and geophysical surveys to refine the deposit’s shape and guide further drilling.

Markets still price about a 93% chance of a 25 bp hike at the Fed's December meeting. WSJ attributes the rate expectations to the AI boom, which has drawn large equity inflows, lifted US growth and revived inflation pressure. Geopolitical risks add safe-haven demand Fundamentals and sentiment suggest that somewhat lower prices are more likely, and that upside may be limited. Just like the US stock market, it is impossible to say that we are getting a significant bottom now just because we see a rally, even if it looks quite strong. Only time will tell. body: Oil fell, as investors unwound hedges against a weekend escalation by US forces in Iran amid signs Washington is taking a more dovish stance for now. West Texas Intermediate declined 4.5% to settle near $80 a barrel for the first time since August. US President Donald Trump appeared to give diplomacy more time, while indicating to Fox News that he may resume the war next year if talks should fail. The comments effectively extend the timeline Trump laid out before the US midterm elections. Hostilities have flared recently, including several attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Still, crude shipments appear to be flowing out of the Persian Gulf as a chorus of analysts forecast an impending oil glut. "Each weekend that passes without meaningful escalation leaves Monday vulnerable to selling pressure, as geopolitical anxiety tends to build over the course of the week and then fade when the weekend passes without a material disruption," said Rebecca Babin, senior energy trader at CIBC Private Wealth Group. Wider volatility in global markets has also pushed traders away from risk. US stocks are mounting a rebound from a rout sparked by fears over the artificial intelligence trade. Global benchmark Brent has dropped by about a fifth this month after Trump held off on renewed strikes following midterm elections in which his Republican Party suffered steep losses. Still, tensions have gradually heightened. Over the weekend, Iran again attacked Bahrain, which hosts US forces. The supply outlook remains robust for now, though. Bernstein analysts including Neil Beveridge predicted that the global oil market will flip back to a surplus over the next three years as supply growth outpaces demand. The International Energy Agency has forecast a roughly 2 million-barrel-a-day surplus this quarter, while Goldman Sachs Group Inc. has also flagged the risk of a glut next year. Among the unresolved issues in the conflict, Iran is demanding that the US end its naval blockade. Iran's state-backed media suggested the government will try to get more ships through the line, which has kept the Islamic Republic from exporting oil and importing some essential goods. In his Fox interview, Trump warned that any such vessels attempting to test the US position would end up "at the bottom of the sea." There's also been an easing in refined fuel prices, which had rallied even harder than crude as the Iran war throttled fuel exports at the same time that Ukrainian strikes hobbled Russian refineries. "This easing in diesel prices could help alleviate inflation pressures and, in turn, reduce concerns about further interest rate hikes, provided the standoff with Iran does not trigger another supply disruption," said Ole Sloth Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank. Still, Moscow and Kyiv continue to trade attacks on each other's energy infrastructure, with a small refinery in southern Russia suspending operations following overnight drone strikes. body: Brent crude traded below US$90 a barrel, while US crude hovered around US$80, recovering slightly after both benchmarks fell sharply in the previous session to three-month lows FALLING crude oil prices and a softer ringgit against the US dollar presented a mixed outlook for Malaysia's economy on Tuesday, as hopes of renewed diplomatic efforts to end the US-Iran conflict eased energy market concerns while expectations of tighter US monetary policy supported the greenback. Brent crude traded below US$90 a barrel, while US crude hovered around US$80, recovering slightly after both benchmarks fell sharply in the previous session to three-month lows. The decline followed reports of renewed diplomatic contacts, including talks between US Vice-President JD Vance and Qatar's prime minister on possible negotiations with Tehran. US President Donald Trump has also delayed further strikes on Iran following the US midterm elections, although he warned that military action could resume after the new year if negotiations fail. However, prospects for a resolution remain uncertain, with Iran demanding the removal of the US naval blockade and sanctions before fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Crude shipments through the strategic waterway have also weakened. Kpler data showed average flows of about 9.5 million barrels per day in the 10 days to Nov 19, compared with 12.2 million bpd in October. The decline in oil prices could ease pressure on Malaysia's fuel-related import costs, although prolonged disruption to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz remains a risk to global energy supply and price stability. On the currency front, the ringgit traded at 4.1220 against the US dollar, down 0.02 per cent from the previous session. The exchange rate had declined 0.88 per cent over the past four weeks, although the ringgit remained 0.30 per cent stronger against the greenback over the past 12 months. The US Dollar Index stood at 104.305, down marginally by 0.01 per cent on the day, but had gained 4.66 per cent over the past year. The dollar's recent strength was supported by easing concerns over the artificial intelligence sector, following a recovery in technology shares and broader equity markets after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive. Expectations that the US Federal Reserve may need to raise interest rates further to contain persistent inflation have also underpinned the greenback. Markets were pricing in a roughly 96 per cent probability of a 25-basis-point rate increase in December, compared with 99 per cent early last week, while traders continued to anticipate another increase in January. Investors are now awaiting the US personal consumption expenditures inflation report this week for further indications of underlying price pressures and the Fed's monetary policy direction. Analysts' forecasts put the US Dollar Index at 103.609 by the end of this quarter and 102.032 in one year, while the US dollar-ringgit exchange rate is projected at 4.10428 and 4.03889 over the same periods, respectively. - November 24, 2026

body: The rand remained under pressure against major currencies on Monday, as investors weighed renewed US dollar strength, weaker precious metal prices in recent weeks and uncertainty surrounding South Africa’s municipal coalition negotiations . The local currency was trading at R17.52 against the dollar on Monday afternoon, gaining 0.31% on the day. It was also firmer against the pound at R22.92, up 0.37%, and the euro at R19.17, gaining 0.55%. Gold was trading at $3 615.97 an ounce, rising 2.34%, while Brent crude declined 1.27% to $91.39 a barrel. The currency movements come as global markets attempt to recover from a sharp sell-off in technology shares on Friday, when concerns about artificial intelligence (AI) valuations triggered significant losses on Wall Street. Bianca Botes, managing director at Citadel Global, said global markets opened the week recovering from Friday’s technology sell-off, which was the worst since 2020. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28% on Friday, erasing its gains for 2026, while Nvidia lost 14% despite reporting a 103% increase in quarterly revenue. The S&P 500 declined 3.70% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.93%. The VIX volatility index, which measures expected market volatility, rose above 35. Asian markets followed Wall Street lower on Monday. South Korea’s KOSPI declined 3.3%, while the MSCI AC Asia Pacific index fell 0.3%. Japan’s Nikkei was closed for Labour Thanksgiving Day. However, US futures rebounded between 2% and 3%, suggesting some tentative stabilisation after Friday’s sell-off. Botes said the recovery in gold and other precious metals could support the local market. “With gold demand and futures higher, we can expect a firmer open for the JSE All Share off Friday's 52 week low, though the market’s risk appetite remains fragile,” she said. Gold was trading more than 2% higher on Monday, recovering from a recent 14-month low. Platinum and other platinum group metals were also holding firmer, while Brent crude remained around the $90 a barrel mark. The global market uncertainty has also influenced expectations around US monetary policy. Botes said demand for safe-haven assets had pushed the yield on the 10-year US Treasury bond down to 4.94%, while expectations of a Federal Reserve interest rate increase in December had eased. The US Dollar Index was holding broadly steady near 103.8, while investors were awaiting economic data that could influence the outlook for US interest rates. Flash purchasing managers’ index figures from the US, eurozone and the UK were due on Monday, ahead of Wednesday’s US core personal consumption expenditures inflation data, an important measure watched by the Federal Reserve. Maarten Ackerman, chief economist at CAM Asset Management, said the rand’s recent weakness had largely been driven by expectations of significant interest rate increases in the US following higher inflation. He said the stronger dollar had coincided with a deterioration in South Africa’s trade account, reducing the support the country had previously received from higher commodity prices. “The dollar has strengthened considerably, while our trade account has also weakened substantially, with much less support coming from higher gold and platinum prices,” Ackerman said. He added that lower gold prices had placed further pressure on the rand, while South Africa was also paying more for oil. “As a result, the trade tailwind we benefited from last year has shifted from a surplus into a deficit,” he said. Ackerman said political uncertainty had also contributed to pressure on the currency, although these effects were often relatively short-lived. With municipal coalition negotiations expected to provide greater clarity towards the end of the week, he said there could be some relief for the rand, depending on the outcome. body: Gold has corrected sharply from its record high earlier this year, leaving investors and jewellery buyers wondering whether the worst is over. Its next move could depend on three US economic events in the coming weeks: the October PCE inflation report on 25 November, the November jobs report on 4 December and the US Federal Reserve’s policy decision on 9 December. All three could shape the Fed’s interest rate path and outlook, which in turn affects global bullion prices . Gold has fallen about 31.7% from its January record of ₹ 1.83 lakh per 10 grams. On 23 November, 99.9% pure gold traded at ₹ 1,25,030 per 10 grams in New Delhi, a minor recovery after seven straight sessions of losses. A stronger US dollar, rising Treasury yields and expectations of further Fed rate hikes have weighed on gold and the wider bullion market. Gold pays no interest, unlike bank fixed deposits and similar investments, so higher interest rates generally reduce its appeal. With these core fundamentals in mind, here are the three dates investors should watch over the next few weeks. The October Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation report is scheduled for release on Wednesday, 25 November. This will provide investors with clear clues about the underlying US price pressure. Core PCE inflation will be a key focus for top investors worldwide. This metric excludes food and energy prices and provides real insights. It is released by the US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). Then next will be the November employment report, which will be released on Friday, 4 December. This is yet another critical report that will indicate whether the US labour market continues to hold and stays resilient. This is a vital metric because strong job creation could reinforce expectations of tighter monetary conditions, whereas signs of weakness may support the bullion market and gold demand. After these two important events, the most closely watched will be the Federal Reserve’s policy announcement, scheduled for Wednesday, 9 December. During this, investors will analyse and assess not just the interest rate decision but also policymakers’ guidance on future rate movements. For Indian gold investors and aspiring buyers, it is essential to keep in mind that domestic gold prices are influenced by international bullion rates, the rupee-dollar exchange rate and import duties. Hence, movements in the US dollar and global gold prices, along with how geopolitical developments related to the US-Iran war pan out, can directly influence and affect Indian gold buyers and investors. Moreover, any further correction in precious metal prices, especially gold, might offer aspiring jewellery buyers and investors an opportunity to invest at lower levels. Still, investors should remember that volatility and significant price fluctuations can continue around major economic announcements and geopolitical developments. These three dates could show whether gold’s correction extends or gives way to a recovery. Rather than assuming prices have bottomed out, investors should track the data and the Fed’s signals, and seek professional advice before investing. title: Will gold prices fall or rise? Watch these eight dates - The Financial Express
body: When gold prices rise, many people delay their purchases and wait for a fall. When prices drop, others wait to see if they will fall further. But how can buyers understand which way the market might move? US economic reports can offer some clues. Inflation, employment, economic growth and interest-rate decisions can all influence international gold prices. These reports follow a schedule. Buyers and investors can use release dates to prepare for potential market moves. However, a report's release date does not tell us whether gold prices will rise or fall. The key is to compare the actual figures with market expectations. Gold is traded internationally in US dollars. Its price is therefore linked to the strength of the dollar, US interest rates and government bond yields. When US interest rates rise, bonds and other interest-bearing investments become more attractive. Gold does not pay interest. Some investors may therefore sell gold and move their money into these assets. This can push gold prices down. The opposite can happen when interest rates fall, or investors expect rate cuts. A weaker dollar and lower bond yields can also support gold prices. Recent market movements offer an example. In October, US consumer inflation rose 0.4 per cent, above the market forecast of 0.3 per cent, according to the US Bureau of Labour Statistics (BLS). Core inflation also rose 0.3 per cent, above the expected 0.2 per cent. The figures strengthened the dollar and pushed Treasury yields higher. Spot gold fell 2.7 per cent to $4,028.39 per ounce on November 10, Reuters reported. Several US agencies publish economic reports every month. Here are eight releases scheduled between late November and mid-December 2026 that could influence the gold market. The Conference Board publishes the Consumer Confidence Index every month. It measures how consumers feel about the economy, job opportunities and their financial situation. A higher-than-expected reading could suggest that the US economy remains strong. This may reduce expectations of interest-rate cuts and put pressure on gold prices. The US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) publishes Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation data in its Personal Income and Outlays report. Investors pay close attention to Core PCE. It excludes food and energy prices because they tend to fluctuate more. For example, if the expected monthly core inflation figure is 0.2 per cent but the actual figure reaches 0.4 per cent, investors may expect fewer Fed rate cuts. The dollar and bond yields could rise, putting pressure on gold. Lower-than-expected inflation could have the opposite effect. It may increase expectations of rate cuts and support gold prices. The BEA is also scheduled to publish its second estimate of US GDP growth for the third quarter of 2026. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures the total value of goods and services produced in an economy. It helps investors assess economic growth. Stronger-than-expected growth could reduce expectations of interest-rate cuts. This may put downward pressure on gold. Weaker growth could increase those expectations and support gold prices. The BLS publishes the Job Openings and Labour Turnover Survey (JOLTS). It provides data on job vacancies, hiring, and workers leaving their jobs. A higher-than-expected number of job openings could point to a strong labour market. This may reduce expectations of rate cuts and put pressure on gold. The monthly Employment Situation report is one of the most closely watched US economic releases. The BLS publishes data on nonfarm payrolls, unemployment and average hourly earnings. If job creation exceeds expectations, investors may see it as a sign of a strong labour market. This could give the Federal Reserve more reason to keep interest rates high. body: Global gold prices are one of the investment instruments whose movements are shaped by various global economic dynamics. Changes in United States monetary policy, the value of the US dollar, and geopolitical developments all help determine the direction of this precious metal’s price. After breaking back above US$4,000 per troy ounce, gold prices remain a focus for market participants. The US$4,000 per troy ounce level is an important support area, while US$4,200 could act as resistance. These two levels can serve as a reference for understanding gold price movements amid various market sentiments. A number of factors affect gold’s appeal and the outlook for global gold prices, ranging from interest rate policy to global gold demand. What are the 5 factors you should know about? Let’s find out! The interest rate policy of the Federal Reserve, or the Fed, is one of the factors that influence global gold price movements. The US central bank’s decisions on interest rates help shape financial market conditions and affect the appeal of various investment instruments, including gold. The Fed is expected to potentially raise interest rates by 25 basis points in December. This expectation is in line with the still fairly strong US labor market and inflation that has not yet come close to the 2% target. If a rate hike materializes, interest-bearing assets such as US government bonds could offer increasingly attractive yields. When the dollar strengthens, gold becomes relatively more expensive for buyers using other currencies. This can affect demand and put pressure on gold prices. Conversely, a weaker US dollar could make gold more attractive to global buyers. This situation can support gold prices, especially when accompanied by positive market sentiment. A weaker US dollar is one of the factors that can drive global gold prices higher. body: Nvidia shares surged 31.48%, adding roughly $952 billion in market capitalization after the board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and president. This move alleviates key-person risk, stabilizes internal morale, and ensures continuity for next-generation platforms like Rubin. Wall Street firms responded positively; Bernstein upgraded the stock to Outperform with a $200 price target, while Citi raised its target to $240. Despite renewed confidence in AI infrastructure demand, some analysts remain cautious. Ongoing board investigations, U.S. regulatory scrutiny, and an upcoming congressional hearing introduce corporate governance risks and potential valuation discounts until regulatory outcomes are finalized. TradingKey - Jensen Huang's return to the helm of Nvidia ( NVDA ) quickly reversed market concerns over the continuity of the company's leadership and product strategy. On Monday, Nvidia's board unanimously agreed to reinstate Huang as president, chief executive officer, and director. Following the announcement, the company's stock surged 31.48%, marking its largest single-day gain since May 2003 and its third-strongest single-day performance since listing, adding approximately $952 billion to its market capitalization in a single day. When Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara, California, he was greeted by hundreds of employees. He remarked on-site that he would 'do better in my second stint as CEO.' The remarks temporarily stabilized internal morale and signaled to customers, suppliers, and investors that the company's technology roadmap would not be disrupted by management changes. Huang's return eased investor concerns over the stability of Nvidia's leadership and prompted multiple Wall Street firms to reevaluate the stock's outlook. However, analysts have not reached a consensus of optimism. Some institutions believe core management risks have been eliminated and the stock still has upside potential. Meanwhile, other analysts caution that the board's investigation and related scrutiny by U.S. regulators have not yet concluded, and corporate governance issues could still weigh on valuations. Over the past few weeks, investors were concerned that a leadership transition could affect the rollout pace of next-generation platforms such as Rubin, as well as the company's partnerships with cloud service providers, chip suppliers, and AI labs. With Jensen Huang now back at the helm, this uncertainty has notably subsided. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon swiftly upgraded Nvidia to Outperform from Market Perform while maintaining a $200 price target. The firm had downgraded the stock just 11 days earlier due to Huang's departure, and now, with management risk reversed, the rating has been restored. Rasgon believes that the long-term fundamentals of AI infrastructure buildout remain unchanged, and Huang's return reestablishes the company's strategic direction. Nvidia continues to hold a leading edge in GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, networking equipment, and full systems, while also possessing the capability to translate its next-generation product roadmap into revenue growth. Citi analyst Atif Malik likewise viewed Huang's reinstatement as a major positive, maintaining a Buy rating and raising his price target on NVDA to $240. In Malik's view, Huang's return not only ends the uncertainty surrounding the CEO transition, but also improves visibility into Nvidia's product roadmap. Customers can proceed with deploying next-generation AI infrastructure as originally planned, and supply chain partners will not need to reassess their long-term capacity arrangements. Stifel analyst Ruben Roy reiterated a Buy rating and a $205 price target, noting that prior market concerns that Huang's departure could weaken the company's technical decision-making efficiency and customer relationships have now been significantly mitigated. title: Jensen Huang’s Return As Nvidia CEO Sparks AI Stock Rally, But Congressional Probes Loom – And Analysts See Risks Ahead - TradingView
body: The reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) CEO triggered a sharp rally in the company’s shares as well as the broader tech market. However, some commentators said the move is a net positive, but risks remain, and the outcome of the government investigation will provide greater clarity on the long-term outlook. NVDA stock rose 31.5% on Monday after the Nvidia board announced the return of Huang, and gained a further 0.5% in overnight trading. Intel (AMD), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Broadcom (AVGO) and iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) gained sharply as well but fell in overnight trading. Hyperscaler Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet (GOOGL) kept their gains overnight. “The NVIDIA board’s brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed,” said a joint statement by the Select Committee on China, Select Committee on Intelligence, and Foreign Affairs Committee, which is investigating Nvidia and Huang over the spy crisis. Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter will appear for hearings on Dec. 1 and Dec. 2, respectively. “We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities," the statement read. The California state and the Securities and Exchange Commission are also investigating the AI chip giant for various alleged infringements. Huang’s reappointment marks a dramatic turn of events. He was ousted after his multiple affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, came to light, and the Nvidia board had said last week that it had no plans to bring him back. The board reversed its position on Monday, hours after President Donald Trump posted in support of Huang’s reinstatement. The development reinforces that Huang is a special leader and Nvidia is a special company but also flags questions, said Wharton professor Mohamed A. El-Erian. “While today’s news answers one set of questions, it raises another set that, similarly, ranges from the narrow (Nvidia’s governance process) to the broad (implications for markets, presidential put, government intervention, national champions, etc.),” he said in an X post. Noted Nvidia critic and “Big Short Investor” Michael Burry said Nvidia is hardly out of the woods. “So $NVDA is weaker, more craven than even I thought. @TheJusticeDept stay on that antitrust case. @SECGov keep digging into that accounting. Godspeed,” he said in an X post. On the other hand, Deepwater Asset Management’s Gene Munster said he was not surprised with the stock's sharp rally on Monday. “The reason is the fundamentals of the AI trade are stronger than what we thought on Nov 5 with Nvidia raising next years guide by 5%. Even with China revenue that will get scrubbed the underlying message remains: we’re early in AI,” he said in an X post. “$NVDA is still 11% lower than post-Blue Wave selloff. I think it’s fair it closes that gap back to $182,” he said. CNBC’s Jim Cramer said: “Look it was a hasty investigation and then a hanging. Jensen welcome back.” On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for NVDA climbed higher in the ‘extremely bullish’ zone. At least 64% of nearly 25,000 traders who voted in an ongoing Stocktwits poll said they feel more bullish about Nvidia after Huang’s return. Fifteen percent said they felt the same as before and 12% voted saying it is too early to tell. “From the companies perspective it's good news.. but let's see what happens when the investigation gets fully underway, 1st week of December will be interesting,” a trader commented. “Honestly I expect there is more we don't know yet. im not ready to jump back in personally.” Despite Monday’s rally, NVDA stock remained 11.3% lower year to date.

XPU shipments rose more than 3.5 times and accounted for approximately 73% of AI semiconductor revenue in the third quarter. AI networking revenue grew more than 2.5 times. Broadcom expects fourth-quarter AI revenue of $21.7 billion, up 236% from a year earlier. The forecast reflects higher accelerator shipments for Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and Meta. The company expects both XPU and AI networking revenue to triple from a year earlier. Management raised its FY26 AI revenue forecast to approximately $58 billion, representing 186% growth. Broadcom expects AI revenue to reach $115 billion in FY27 and $230 billion in FY28. The company says it has secured the supply needed to support those targets. Memory chipmakers did the heavy lifting, with SK Hynix up about 8.6% and Samsung Electronics up about 8.2%. The rebound came a day after Seoul said it was ready to activate a market stabilisation fund of about 10.8 trillion won. title: Bessent blames Lutnick’s Commerce as he slams Nvidia chip ‘leakage’ to China
summary: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO days after admitting to an affair following scrutiny of his relationship with a woman reportedly deemed a Chinese spy.
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration have long supported imposing restrictions on Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's spy-sex scandal . But the Commerce Department is in charge "and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC's " Squawk Box ." The Cabinet secretary's comments hinting at disunity within the administration followed an Axios report that Bessent, in the White House Situation Room last week, had asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed. Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported. Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation" in the Situation Room. Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room." But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months." Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s." "And so any leakage is very frustrating" because it "hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. Huang, seen as one of Trump's closest corporate allies, resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday after admitting to an affair following scrutiny of his relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly determined to be a Chinese spy. Huang had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales. Asked if he believes Nvidia's highest-level processors have made it to China using the Singapore-based Megaspeed as a pass-through, Bessent said, "I think that there is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down." "The story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles," Bessent told CNBC. "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?" "I think it's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that," he said. The Commerce Department did not respond to CNBC's request for comment on Bessent's remarks. Huang and Lutnick both have been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month, Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Thursday . Eichamer, the Commerce spokeswoman, told CNBC on Friday that Lutnick "has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions." Huang has separately been asked to sit for a closed-door briefing on Dec. 1 before the House committees on China, intelligence and foreign affairs. The Republican chairmen of those panels have also asked Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter to participate in a closed-door interview with them on Dec. 2. House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., separately asked Jeff Kessler, Commerce's under secretary for industry and security, to appear before his committee on Dec. 3 for a hearing on "chip smuggling, adversary military use of advanced AI chips, reported interference by private companies into export control policy and enforcement investigations."

The recent washout completely cleaned out roughly 18,000 outstanding non-commercial contracts on the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, compared to a peak of about 1.5 lakh contracts. title: Jensen Huang faces DC grilling the same day Nvidia releases new products at GTC
summary: Jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia and immediately faces the challenge of leading the chip giant and defending himself in Washington.
body: Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia , and is now tasked with selling the company's artificial intelligence vision while also defending himself in Washington. As Nvidia employees celebrated the return of their leader to the company's headquarters, Huang told the gathered crowd, "I'll be a better CEO the second time around." Huang will need to be a better CEO to head off the issues surrounding Nvidia and the broader AI industry exposed by Huang's exit. The challenges include a proliferating roster of investigations and hearings from Congress, regulators and state-level officials , as well as technical and competitive questions about how long Nvidia's currently dominant graphics processing units can remain on top. "There's nothing prohibiting him from doing what he does on his day job," said Katten chair and former federal prosecutor Gil Soffer. But investigations take significant prep time, Soffer said. "You don't just walk in cold." At Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, D.C., next week, the company will attempt to convince customers, partners and suppliers that it is developing the future of AI. At the same time, lawmakers will be pressing its newly reinstated CEO over what he knew and when about Megaspeed executive Alice Huang . Huang, before his scandals, was scheduled to give the GTC DC keynote speech on Dec. 1 to discuss new Nvidia products and the trajectory of the AI ecosystem. In the past, the two-hour speech was the highlight of the event with hordes of fans full of the Huang-inspired "Jensanity." "People will want to see that it's business as usual, which hopefully for Nvidia shareholders will mean that Jensen Huang announces some new exciting products," said Babson College associate professor Peter Cohan. Right now, Nvidia has Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, filling the slot. A representative for Nvidia declined to answer multiple questions about whether Huang would appear at the company's event. On the same day, Huang is scheduled to speak with three House committees — Foreign Affairs, Select Committee on the CCP, and the Select Committee on Intelligence — behind closed doors, where his interview will be transcribed. "The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the chairs said in a joint statement. They said that Huang has confirmed he will appear for the transcribed interview on Dec. 1. Next Tuesday's interviews are just the first of a slew of investigations. On Dec. 3, just as Nvidia's conference is wrapping up, the Senate Banking Committee will hold a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls." Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the committee, said Huang will publicly testify as the sole witness. California's attorney general is also investigating Huang's remarks, and politicians from the Senate Finance, Intelligence, and Foreign Relations committees have inquired about the scandal. In the House, Energy and Commerce has requested a company briefing from Nvidia, in addition to the three committees mentioned earlier. That's not counting an investigation from the Department of Justice and a reported investigation from the Securities and Exchange Commission . Plus, Huang still has to cooperate with an investigation from the board of directors, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton. Meanwhile, Nvidia needs Huang to reassure investors and the broader AI ecosystem that the company is developing new products that will be in high demand. Investors had said that while Nvidia's products for the next two years have been fully designed, they were worried that the chipmaker's pace of innovation would slow without Huang. Nvidia is facing new competition from chips from its biggest customers, including OpenAI , Anthropic , Google , Amazon and Microsoft . title: Anthropic stock falls below $83 IPO price, but analysts are still largely positive
summary: Anthropic has been sinking steadily since the stock opened at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Nov. 19.
body: Shares of Anthropic fell 8% on Tuesday, sending the stock below the artificial intelligence company's $83 IPO price. The AI lab's stock has been sinking steadily since opening at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Thursday, after Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest offering of all time. Investors eagerly awaited Anthropic's debut in hopes that the company would revitalize the broader AI trade, which has been volatile in recent weeks over concerns about the feasibility of a multitrillion-dollar infrastructure buildout. Chip stocks Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices and Intel , as well as neoclouds CoreWeave , IREN and Nebius , all fell during intraday trading on Tuesday. The market is still reeling after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, a dramatic reversal from his ouster earlier this month. Nvidia shares surged more than 30% on Monday, but pared those gains Tuesday. Analysts at Canaccord Genuity said Tuesday that they're focused on Anthropic's long-term potential. They said they believe that the company is building "one of the most important enterprise technology franchises of the AI era" and that the "opportunity is considerably larger than traditional software spending." Canaccord Genuity initiated coverage of Anthropic with a buy rating and a $135 price target. "The risks are unusually large, particularly around infrastructure commitments and the durability of competitive differentiation, but we believe the combination of exceptional growth, emerging earnings capacity, and an attractive entry valuation support a compelling investment opportunity," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note. Wedbush analysts initiated coverage of Anthropic with an outperform rating and a $120 price target on Monday. They said Anthropic went public in a "tumultuous market" as debate around the AI buildout continues, but that they expect the company to navigate the competitive environment and "capture a uniquely large addressable market." "While there's going to continue to be many ups and downs, and winners and losers as this ecosystem gets built, in our view there is no real question that it does get built over time," the analysts wrote in a Monday note. "The genie is out of the bottle. And ANT is a strong play on that theme." Analysts at Oppenheimer initiated coverage of Anthropic with an outperform rating on Tuesday, and they set a $150 price target for the stock. They said their "bullish stance" on the company stems from their belief that Anthropic will capture growing enterprise AI spending, that its improving compute efficiency lowers cost per task and that its multi-chip strategy optimizes price performance. The analysts added that Anthropic's focus on the enterprise also relies less on consumer subsidies, and that rising customer adoption creates "a substantial runway" for the company. "While competition and compute commitments remain risks, we believe Anthropic can translate its leadership into durable growth and operating leverage," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note. title: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO, but investigations and risks remain
summary: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO, but the company still faces an internal investigation and California and federal scrutiny.
body: Jensen Huang has the backing of U.S. President Donald Trump and investors: Nvidia 's stock gained nearly $1 trillion after the abrupt board reversal that reinstated him as CEO. But investigations and governance questions still hang over the chipmaker, and analysts said that internal and external probes of Huang and Nvidia could fuel uncertainty. Trump's intervention to have Huang reinstated, alongside a concerted campaign from investors and employees, saw the Nvidia co-founder return just 11 days after he resigned amid reports of extramarital relationships, including one with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Shares rose 31% Monday and were around 5% lower in Tuesday's premarket trading. It was a dramatic turnaround just days after Nvidia's new board chair, Harvey Jones, rejected calls to reinstate Huang on Nov. 17. Nvidia, which had not responded to a CNBC request for comment as this article went live, is investigating reports that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, which the company said on Monday would continue as it restored him to the top job. California's Department of Justice is probing whether Nvidia's advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public. Reuters reported on Friday that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into the company's accounting practices. The SEC declined to comment. Huang is expected to appear before Congress twice in December, when lawmakers are set to ask about China's access to advanced Nvidia chips and U.S. export controls. Sebastien Naji, analyst at William Blair, said in a note on Monday that Huang's return "clears some of the uncertainty" about the company but "events of recent weeks have exposed deeper questions around corporate governance, leadership succession, and regulatory oversight that could have lasting implications for the company's competitive position." Trump told CNBC Monday that he personally intervened to speak with the board about reinstating Huang. The president posted on Truth Social on Monday that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." David O'Connor, senior research analyst at Piper Sandler, said in a note on Monday that Congress will "likely want their answers" from Huang but, given the U.S. government assurances on national security, "we don't think this will translate into anything meaningful to the stock." The board's investigation is the "key risk" that remains, said Cody Acree, analyst at StoneX, in a note on Monday. He wrote that any conclusion that "confidential information was shared" or that compliance was compromised would "reopen the leadership question." But Acree added that the board's reinstatement of Huang suggested it had "confidence in where the investigation is heading, and the government input it cited lowers the odds of an adverse finding." But scrutiny could slow Nvidia's deal-making, Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at Questar Capital Partners, told CNBC's "Access Middle East" on Tuesday. He called Nvidia "kind of the central bank of the AI trade," adding: "With all the scrutiny they're going to be under, it's going to be very difficult for them to have the same level of deal-making capacity out there in the marketplace." Stacy A. Rasgon, managing director at Bernstein, said in a note on Monday that the board faced "legitimate questions as to their judgment and process, which has to make one wonder how they come to their other important decisions." Democrats taking over Congress in January could keep Huang and Nvidia in the "crosshairs," Rasgon added. Members of Congress from both parties doubled down on their calls for investigations into the company, as they expressed anger at Huang's return.
