title: Property Play: Commercial real estate activity falls 14% in October, as interest rates rise
summary: Commercial real estate activity dropped 14% in October from September, according to an index from LightBox, a commercial real estate data platform.
body: Interest rates moved higher in September, and that had a swift impact on commercial real estate deal-making. After settling in the low-to-mid-4% range, the yield on the 10-year Treasury moved above 5% and has been wavering around there with the potential to move even higher due to stubborn inflation. As a result, commercial real estate activity dropped 14% in October from September, according to an index from LightBox, a commercial real estate data platform. Of the index's three components, commercial property listings fell 20% from September, environmental site assessments were down 1% and lender appraisals dropped 11%. The appraisal measure is at its weakest level of the three and is now down 17% from a year ago. It shows that both lenders and borrowers are stepping back, unable to pencil deals and move from listing to closing. "What makes this so interesting is that during tariffs, it didn't dip. During $100 oil earlier this year, it didn't dip. When we saw interest rates marching up the first half of this year, it didn't dip. In fact, it kind of increased, and now we've fallen off a map in October," said Manus Clancy, head of data strategy at LightBox. "It's like we've reached this straw that has broken the camel's back in terms of people saying, 'Okay, enough is enough. I can't keep putting money to work without some clarity on where interest rates are going.'" Clancy said deals were happening earlier this year because investors had gotten more comfortable with where interest rates had settled. The office market was beginning to recover as more companies ordered workers back. Multifamily, which had seen a glut of new construction, was also starting to see vacancies fall and rents rise. This takes the market back to 2023, when deal-making froze up because interest rates had shot up sharply from very low, pandemic-induced levels. As property values repriced, the gap between what the sellers wanted and what the buyers were willing to pay widened. That is what is happening now. Whether they are refinancing a loan or getting a new loan to purchase a property, investors, developers and property owners are now deciding to wait to see if interest rates come down at all. While the Federal Reserve is expected to raise its lending rate further, an end to the war with Iran could bring Treasury yields down. Especially for refinances, borrowers would be out millions of dollars at these higher rates. On the buy side, deals simply don't work anymore at higher rates. "I think it is disorienting as people try to rebase values, and in the midst of transactions, you're seeing value retrades at the 11th hour, deals getting pulled, and volume slowing down yet again in the market," said Ryan Cotton, head of real estate at Bain Capital in a recent Property Play podcast . "It's definitely a confusing and complicated time to be a real estate investor." Higher interest rates were the leading factor for the slowdown in October, but LightBox cited another contributing factor. Lending remains open, but sentiment has weakened. It points to the Mortgage Bankers Association cutting its 2027 growth forecast for commercial mortgage lending from about 8% to 1%. In addition, the Commercial Real Estate Finance Council, or CREFC, Sentiment Index fell 17.5% in the third quarter of this year to a three-year low. "People are lending for construction. They're lending for office conversion. They're lending for new purchases," noted Clancy. "We look at this index as kind of the tip of the spear. That if something's going to go sideways, this is the first indicator that people are stopping the ordering of appraisals, and we think that this portends that the next quarter will show a lot of decline in bank lending on commercial real estate." title: Does the Nvidia-led rip mark the market bottom? Maybe not
summary: The standard market playbook is to assume that we’ve put in “a low, not the final low.”
body: The key accelerant to Monday's ripping rebound was a shocker. But the level that halted the rally was right where you'd expect. The S&P 500's 4.7% surge on Monday lifted it out of a steep-sided hole following last week's washout selling storm. Its high for the day was just under 7300, a level last seen on Thursday, corresponding to the index's summertime low and representing the floor of the former multi-month trading range. In other words, the pop stopped at the point from which the tape had broken down; the index slipped three-quarters of a percent from there by the close. More than a third of the S&P's gain was provided by the 31% jump in Nvidia shares alone following Jensen Huang's stunning reinstatement as Nvidia CEO. Here, too, the stock closed right near the Iran-selloff low, which it cracked through some 12 days ago. It remains under all the relevant moving averages and trend lines. This isn't to minimize or denigrate these moves of rare magnitude, but simply to place them in context. The market was going to attempt a solid bounce no matter the news. S&P 500 futures were indicated higher by more than 2% even before the Huang bombshell struck before Monday's open. By near-universal agreement, last week's flush had generated the kind of indiscriminate liquidation, oversold conditions and urgent hedging that typically set up at least a snapback rip. Some of these readings were as extreme as near the April 2025 low following the tariff panic, though not all. The reinstallation of Huang at the apparent behest of the White House triggered an emotional, spring-loaded ramp in the AI trade, a collective panic by the under-invested. When the government jolts the market with a policy shift like this, it not only assuages a prevailing fear in the market, but it grants psychic permission to investors who were frantically selling one day to ravenously buy back the same stocks the next. It's slightly ironic, given that a common line last week on the recent market setback was that – unlike in the tariff panic or the Iran war corrections – there was no single policy reversal that could short-circuit the selloff and trigger a ferocious recovery. And maybe there still isn't. Such one-day comebacks from a deeply oversold state are to be respected but not fully trusted. Looking back at prior one-day gains of such amplitude – or prior sequences of a daily drop and gain of more than 5% in the Nasdaq-100 – generate a fair number of episodes inside of nasty bear markets, along with a few consequential market bottoms. A few further observations and questions at a potentially tenuous tactical moment for the markets: -The standard playbook is to assume that we've put in "a low, not the final low." Oversold rallies can carry on a while – say, to the 20-day moving average, which for the S&P 500 is up another 3% from here – without getting escape velocity. Graybeards argue for keeping the market on a short leash, expecting there will at least be a retest sequence. Prudent to assume so, though it's inescapable that V-shaped bottoms have become a bit more common in recent years, as recently as at the end of March, on the merest hint that President Trump would consider ceasing Iran hostilities without forcing open the Strait of Hormuz. -Index corrections of at least 10% that happen quickly have generally been more associated with temporary bull-market dips than the start of nastier downturns. This latest S&P 500 correction happened over 33 trading days, among the dozen quickest. That would be reassuring, except that places it right between the declines of November 2007 and February 2022, which indeed were the start of bear markets. -Remember that the pain of this setback was inflicted after months in which Wall Street was constantly extolling the virtues of a "broadening" market (equal-weight S&P 500 outperforming) and marveling at the elegant rotation into "quality" and defensive stocks that was supporting the S&P 500. Two months ago, the series was at the lowest since 2014. That said, last week's major retailer earnings and commentary was positive on the macro side. Today, retail comps came in solid. Abercrombie was next at +6%, with every region accelerating, then Dollar Tree at +4.6% on 3.8% traffic growth and Kohl's at +1.2%, its first top-line growth in more than four years. The macro read is less clean. Best Buy's blended ASPs rose 6% with units flat, and computing prices jumped 25% on memory costs while units fell mid-teens. That's goods inflation flattering nominal sales, and HPE says memory supply stays tight into H2 2028. Dollar Tree's traffic points to continued trade-down. Tariff refunds flattered margins everywhere and Dollar Tree is putting some of that money into lower prices, but none of it repeats in Q4. Best Buy's 2-4% Q4 comp guide says the pace is already cooling. “Consumer confidence rallied again in November, potentially due to lower uncertainty following the midterm elections,” said Fergus McCormick, Senior Economist, Global Indicators, The Conference Board. “After two months of consecutive increases, the headline index is back to levels of confidence last seen in January 2025. The gain in confidence was led by stronger perceptions of present and future labor market conditions. Perceptions of current and future business conditions also improved sharply. Along with the gain in headline confidence, consumers planned slightly higher spending on goods and vacations.” For background, the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index is released at 10 am ET on the last Tuesday of each month, making it the final major read on US household sentiment before the month closes. It's benchmarked to 100 in 1985 and is one of two headline sentiment gauges, alongside the University of Michigan survey. The index combines consumers' views on current conditions with their outlook for the next six months. The Present Situation Index reflects how people assess business conditions and the job market today. The Expectations Index captures their outlook for business conditions, employment and household income six months ahead. The Conference Board has long noted that an Expectations Index below 80 has historically signaled a recession within the following year. Its biggest distinction from the Michigan survey is a heavier focus on jobs. The most closely watched detail is the labor differential, the share of respondents who say jobs are "plentiful" minus the share who say jobs are "hard to get." It tracks the unemployment rate closely and often turns before the official labor data, which makes it a useful cross-check ahead of the monthly payrolls report. The survey also covers 12-month inflation expectations, expectations for interest rates and stock prices, and plans to buy homes, vehicles and big-ticket appliances. Open-ended responses show what's weighing on consumers, whether prices, tariffs, politics or job security. Confidence measures have a loose relationship with actual spending, and consumers frequently keep spending even when they report feeling gloomy. Markets usually react only to large surprises. The report's main value is in its labor market detail and in tracking how households are responding to inflation, gasoline prices and the jobs picture heading into the holiday shopping season. body: The US housing market is bad but it's not getting worse, despite rising interest rates. For background, the S&P Case-Shiller Home Price Indices and the Federal Housing Finance Agency's House Price Index are the two main measures of US house prices. Both are released at 9 am ET on the last Tuesday of the month and carry a two-month lag, so the November reports cover September. The Case-Shiller 20-City Composite is the most widely cited. It tracks single-family home prices across 20 major metropolitan areas, including New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Miami, Dallas, Phoenix, Seattle, Boston and Atlanta. S&P also publishes a 10-city composite, a national index and readings for each metro, which often show wide regional gaps. In recent years, the Northeast and Midwest have generally outperformed parts of the Sun Belt and West, where new supply has grown faster. Each monthly figure is a three-month moving average, which smooths the data but adds to the lag. Markets focus on the unadjusted year-over-year change. The FHFA index covers homes bought with conforming mortgages purchased or guaranteed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. That makes it a better gauge of the mainstream market, since it excludes jumbo loans and most cash purchases, which skew toward high-end and investor buying. FHFA reports seasonally adjusted monthly changes and annual changes nationally, for nine census divisions and for states. Both indexes use a repeat-sales method, comparing sale prices of the same homes over time. That controls for shifts in the mix of homes being sold, a weakness of median price measures like the one in NAR's existing home sales report. The two usually point in the same direction, though differences in coverage and weighting mean the size of the moves can vary. Because the data are stale by the time they're released, neither report moves markets much. Their value is in tracking the long-run trend in home values, which drives household wealth and confidence. Mortgage rates, tight inventory and the lock-in effect have been the main forces shaping prices. Your market education doesn't end here. body: Iraq Refuses to Accept OPEC+ Assessment of its Production Capacity Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… Iraq is refusing to accept an OPEC+ assessment that says the country can sustainably produce less than 5 million barrels of oil per day. Baghdad wants OPEC+ to recognize a capacity of around 6 million bpd—an important acknowledgment ahead of the group’s upcoming Sunday meeting, at which production targets for 2027 are expected to be a topic of discussion. Under the current OPEC+ production agreement, Iraq's limit is 4.431 million bpd. If OPEC acknowledges the higher capacity assessment that Iraq is requesting, it would give Baghdad a stronger argument for a larger quota. OPEC+ hired outside consultants to assess members' production capabilities before deciding how much oil each country should be permitted to pump. Granting Iraq a larger allocation would mean either allowing more oil onto the market or reducing the amount other members can produce. Earlier this month, Iraq’s Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair claimed that Iraq was already producing more than 5 million bpd, which is higher than the quota. He also insisted Iraq was complying with OPEC+ requirements because its exports remained within acceptable limits. But OPEC+ limits don’t set limits on exports, and oil produced for domestic use isn’t exempt from production quotas. According to OPEC's November report, Baghdad reported October production of 4.888 million bpd, which is higher than the current quota. OPEC's independent sources put the figure at 4.491 million bpd. That's a difference of nearly 400,000 barrels daily between what Iraq says it pumped and what OPEC believes it pumped. Even the lower estimate exceeds Iraq's current production allowance by roughly 60,000 bpd. The International Energy Agency estimates Iraq's sustainable production capacity at 4.87 million bpd, considerably below Iraq’s self-assessed 6 million bpd capacity. Iraq threatened earlier this year to leave OPEC if it didn't receive a satisfactory allocation, although it later withdrew that warning. The UAE has already departed the organization over similar issues. body: Iraq Refuses to Accept OPEC+ Assessment of its Production Capacity Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… Saudi Arabia now expects its economy to shrink 2.1% this year instead of 3.6%, after recovering enough oil exports to mitigate some of the damage caused by the Iran war. The revised forecast, announced in Tuesday's budget statement, is a considerable improvement from last month, but before the war began, Saudi Arabia had been expecting economic growth of approximately 4.5%. Saudi oil exports in October were the highest since the war began. Aramco has been moving more crude through its East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea to offset shipments lost through Hormuz. Saudi Arabia is now exporting enough oil to improve its economic forecast, although production is still below prewar levels. Saudi Arabia was also getting much higher prices for the oil it managed to sell. In fact, in the second quarter, oil revenue increased 28% from the previous quarter, even though the country's oil sector had contracted nearly 25%. The higher prices made up for some of the lost production, and now that Saudi Arabia is exporting more oil, the damage to its economy is becoming less severe. The additional export volumes are now helping the broader economy recover, although the government still expects a budget deficit of 245 billion riyals ($65 billion), equivalent to 4.9% of GDP, this year. Non-oil economic activity is expected to grow 2.3%. Saudi Arabia is forecasting a 10.9% economic rebound next year, supported largely by recovering oil production. It expects its budget deficit to narrow to 191 billion riyals ($51 billion). The finance ministry's figures , however, show that most of the projected deficit reduction comes from spending less, rather than collecting substantially more revenue. Government spending is expected to decline by 44 billion riyals next year, while revenue increases by just 11 billion riyals. Saudi public debt is still expected to increase from 1.73 trillion riyals this year to 1.92 trillion in 2027. Houthi attacks continue to threaten infrastructure, and additional capacity to move oil around Hormuz is not expected to enter construction until 2028. title: Iraq Seeks Federal Control Over Disputed Kurdistan Oilfields
summary: The Iraqi government wants oilfields in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region owned by the federally-held North Oil Company to be placed under federal control after uncovering oil smuggling in the northern fields, Iraq’s Oil Minister, Basim Mohammed Khudair, has said. “An investigation has been conducted, the findings of which will yield specific recommendations. body: Iraq Refuses to Accept OPEC+ Assessment of its Production Capacity The Iraqi government wants oilfields in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region owned by the federally-held North Oil Company to be placed under federal control after uncovering oil smuggling in the northern fields, Iraq’s Oil Minister, Basim Mohammed Khudair, has said. “An investigation has been conducted, the findings of which will yield specific recommendations. There have been violations at oil fields belonging to the North Oil Company,” Khudair told Iraqi News Agency INA in an interview , referring to the uncovering of oil-smuggling operations. The fields belonging to the North Oil Company “have been seized” by the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG), in addition to smuggling activities originating from other areas, the minister said. The Iraqi Ministry of Oil believes that “the management of these fields should be federal, under the Ministry’s authority, consistent with how it manages fields in the central and southern regions,” Khudair told INA. “The Prime Minister intends to resolve all outstanding issues and strengthen control over external border crossings by tasking the Iraqi Army with overseeing them, from the north to the south.” The new showdown with the semi-autonomous region of Kurdistan is brewing just as Iraq is drafting and discussing its federal 2027 budget. Every year, the budget earmarks a share for the Kurdistan region. For next year, the share for Kurdistan is kept at 12.5% of total spending in the budget. But it also includes a provision that the KRG supply at least 400,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil to Iraq’s State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) for exports, according to the budget draft seen by Emirati news outlet The National . If KRG cannot export this volume, Kurdistan should deliver the crude to the federal ministry of oil for domestic use, per the budget draft. Meanwhile, Iraq has boosted its crude oil exports via the Turkish Mediterranean port Ceyhan to 500,000 bpd, as OPEC’s second-largest producer has started trucking Basrah crude to the pipeline system to the north. title: Copper price erases Nvidia rebound as investors steer clear of metals
summary: Traders have booked up to 100,000 tonnes of US copper for China, a sign they are losing faith in tariffs, BMO Capital Markets says.
body: Traders have booked up to 100,000 tonnes of US copper for China, a sign they are losing faith in tariffs, BMO Capital Markets says. Copper gave back all of Monday’s artificial intelligence-fuelled gains on Tuesday as investors who dumped metals during the recent AI rout showed little appetite to return, and traders kept moving US stockpiles to China. Comex copper for December delivery fell 3.5% to $5.437 a pound ($11,985 a tonne) in morning trade in New York. A settlement at that level would be the lowest since March 24. The contract settled at $5.634 on Monday, up 2.7% but well off the session high of $5.787 reached after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive. Tuesday’s drop leaves copper 21% below its record settlement of $6.889 on September 9, technically a bear market. The metal is now down 3% this year and 16% in November. Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange was down 3.5% at $12,054 a tonne in official trading after briefly ducking below $12,000, Reuters reports. It had jumped as much as 5.3% on Monday. Investors who sold commodities during the AI rout that followed Huang’s resignation on November 12 are not rushing back. “These investors are not fully reengaging the positions they had pre-event, which includes commodity exposure,” Panmure Liberum analyst Tom Price told Reuters. Many have decided copper is too volatile and are cutting commodity exposure to concentrate on AI stocks, he said. “There are now multiple reasons for the market to short copper,” Aces Zhou, a base metals trader at Hangzhou Chenglian Industrial, told Bloomberg. Beyond the AI narrative, he said, trade flows are starting to reverse as copper leaves the United States, and the factors that supported the metal’s two-year rally are unravelling. Rate hikes and a strong dollar add to the headwinds. Markets are fully pricing a quarter-point increase at the Federal Reserve’s December meeting, which would be the second this year, Bloomberg reports, and the dollar index is at its highest since March 2025, according to BMO Capital Markets. The physical market remains tight, but financial flows have overpowered it, BMO’s analysts wrote after attending Asia Copper Week in Shanghai last week. Visible exchange inventories cover only about two days of consumption, and the Yangshan premium for imports into China climbed from under $100 a tonne to around $500 in a month. Those premiums, together with a narrowing gap between New York and London prices, have prompted traders to book an estimated 30,000 to 100,000 tonnes of US cathode for direct shipment to China, BMO said. The metal, held outside exchange warehouses on the US west coast, takes about two weeks to arrive. The shipments matter less for the tonnage than for what they signal, BMO said: that traders are losing confidence in a tariff decision that would keep US stockpiles sealed off from the rest of the world. Chinese industry players expect President Donald Trump to drop plans for duties on refined copper, while Western participants still lean towards a tariff being imposed. BMO expects the selloff to extend until Washington signals its tariff intentions or prices fall far enough to hit supply, potentially in the $10,000 to $11,000 a tonne range. Trafigura’s cost curve shows about 10% of copper produced by solvent extraction and electrowinning is already losing money at around $13,000, the bank said. BMO stands by its structurally bullish medium-term view. Talks on 2027 treatment charges, the fees miners pay smelters to process concentrate, remain far apart. Antofagasta has reportedly offered around minus $200 a tonne, while China’s Tongling has signalled about minus $80 could be acceptable, according to BMO. This year’s benchmark was set at zero, already a record low, and BMO estimates some Chinese smelters break even on a cash basis at around minus $90. title: Silver miners struggle to close persistent supply gap
summary: Dependence on copper, lead, zinc and gold operations limits the precious metal’s supply response despite record prices.
body: Dependence on copper, lead, zinc and gold operations limits the precious metal’s supply response despite record prices. Peñasquito is the largest individual silver-producing mine, by output. ( Image courtesy of Newmont via Flickr. ) Global silver mine production is expected to remain virtually unchanged this year despite a sixth consecutive annual market deficit, though weakening industrial demand could tip the market into surplus as early as 2027. Demand is forecast to exceed supply by 35 million oz. in 2026, bringing the cumulative shortfall since 2021 to about 746 million oz., according figures from the Silver Institute and research firm Metals Focus . That represents nearly 90% of annual global mine output, projected at 834 million oz. this year. “Peak silver scarcity is clearly in the rear-view mirror,” Deutsche Bank head of metals research Daniel Ghali wrote in a recent report . The prospect of a surplus despite stagnant mine production highlights a structural disconnect between silver prices and supply. Research by GEM Mining Consulting suggests the market’s ability to rebalance hinges more on changes in consumption, recycling and inventories than on miners expanding operations. Between 2021 and 2025, annual silver demand averaged 1.17 billion oz., up 20% from the preceding four-year period, when the market recorded surpluses. Mine output declined by 0.9%, while recycling increased by 15%. The production response to higher prices has historically been limited and delayed. Between 2006 and 2011, inflation-adjusted silver prices surged 172%, while mine output increased by about 18%, according to GEM. The consultancy’s statistical analysis suggests production has a stronger relationship with prices from two or three years earlier than with current market conditions, although the limited number of observations warrants caution. Primary silver mines accounted for just 26.1% of global mine supply in 2025, down from 28.7% in 2019 and the lowest proportion in Metals Focus’ data series. Lead and zinc operations contributed 29.4%, followed by copper mines at 28% and gold operations at 15.9%. “For them, a higher silver price improves revenues, but hardly justifies, on its own, extracting more ore,” Patricio Faúndez of GEM Mining Consulting wrote of operations that produce silver as a byproduct. Silver output from copper mines increased by 24.5% between 2019 and 2025, supported by expanding global copper production, project ramp-ups in Chile and higher grades in Peru. Production from lead and zinc operations declined by 7.3%, while gold-related output edged 2% higher. Chile illustrates the disconnect. Silver production from the country’s copper mines fell by 10% over the same period despite a 95% increase in inflation-adjusted silver prices, according to GEM’s analysis of Chilean Copper Commission data. Dedicated silver operations have also struggled, with output falling by 7.9% between 2019 and 2025 amid declining grades and operational challenges. Metals Focus expects primary mines to add 6.5 million oz. this year, largely through operational improvements in Mexico. Higher prices lifted their margins by 187% in the first half despite a 47% increase in all-in sustaining costs. Even so, the additional ounces would cover less than one-fifth of this year’s projected market shortfall. While silver briefly surpassed $120 per oz. in January, the price rally has accelerated efforts among industrial consumers to reduce their reliance on the metal. Deutsche estimates global silver consumption in solar applications will decline by more than 20% this year, with Chinese demand falling 33%. Manufacturers are adopting thinner electrical contacts, copper-coated silver pastes and alternative cell designs to reduce costs. Silver consumption per solar cell is forecast to fall 17% this year, according to the bank. title: Marimaca gets Sprott’s backing for Chile copper project
summary: The Marimaca oxide project has the potential to produce an average of 43,000 tonnes of copper cathode a year over 13 years.
body: The Marimaca oxide project has the potential to produce an average of 43,000 tonnes of copper cathode a year over 13 years. View of the Marimaca property in Chile. Credit: Marimaca Copper. Developer Marimaca Copper (TSX: MARI; ASX: MC2) has secured investment committee backing from a Sprott (TSX, NYSE: SII) unit for a proposed funding package to help build its flagship copper project in northern Chile. Vancouver-based Marimaca signed a non-binding term sheet with Sprott Resource Lending for up to C$646.6 million ($450 million), including $425 million in senior secured debt, according to a statement Tuesday . Sprott will also make an equity investment of up to $25 million. The first $100 million of the loan would become available after a construction decision, subject to final agreements and other conditions. Sprott must still complete financial and legal due diligence. Marimaca is heading into 2027 “with detailed engineering, site activity and construction preparation set to accelerate” at the oxide project in the coming months, President Nico Cookson said. The Marimaca oxide project, about 45 km from Antofagasta, would cost $587 million to build and produce an average of 43,000 tonnes of copper cathode a year over 13 years, according to Marimaca’s 2025 feasibility study. Marimaca had $127 million in cash and equivalents at Sept. 30. It still has to arrange the rest of the construction financing. The planned open-pit operation would use heap leaching to recover copper. Its location near highways, power lines and the port of Mejillones provides access to existing infrastructure. Marimaca received environmental approval in November 2025 and is pursuing the remaining construction permits. In a report issued last week, National Bank Financial analyst Andrew Dusome pointed to a targeted final investment decision in mid-2027. He also expected Pampa Medina’s first resource estimate in the first half of next year. The 7½-year loan would carry a minimum interest rate of 8.5%. Sprott would charge 5.75 percentage points over the secured overnight financing rate, a United States benchmark, with a floor of 2.75% on the benchmark. Principal repayments would begin on March 31, 2031. The lender would require neither copper-price hedges nor payments tied to production. The terms would allow Marimaca to keep drilling its nearby Pampa Medina copper-silver discovery during construction. Drill hole SPRD-21 cut 102 metres at 1% copper and 5.1 grams silver per tonne from 706 metres downhole, the company reported Nov. 19. Ongoing drilling at Pampa Medina “continues to expand the mineralized area of interest with large step-out holes and prove out the high-grade central zone,” Dusome wrote. He highlighted the project’s “strong upside potential.” Sprott Resource Lending, a wholly owned subsidiary of asset manager Sprott, arranges debt financing for mining companies. In August, Wia Gold (ASX: WIA) agreed non-binding terms with the lender for $360 million in debt and a $15 million equity subscription to help develop Namibia’s Kokoseb gold project. Emerald Resources (ASX: EMR) also signed a mandate with Sprott and Macquarie Bank for a proposed $200 million acquisition facility during the September quarter. Marimaca shares dropped 1.7% to C$5.88 Tuesday afternoon in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$797 million ($557 million). The stock has traded between C$5.53 and C$13.49 in the past year.

title: World Gold Council brings digital gold trading to life
summary: HSBC, J.P. Morgan and StoneX test a new settlement model that could expand bullion’s use as collateral in financial markets.
body: HSBC, J.P. Morgan and StoneX test a new settlement model that could expand bullion’s use as collateral in financial markets. The World Gold Council has completed the first live pilot of a digital settlement system designed to make physical gold easier to trade and use across wholesale financial markets. HSBC, J.P. Morgan and StoneX traded, settled and used fractional ownership of physical bullion as collateral in legally binding transactions through instruments known as Pooled Gold Interests (PGIs), the Council said on Tuesday . ICE Benchmark Administration (IBA) acted as operator and Baton Systems as technology provider. “This is a historic step forward for the gold market, preserving trust in physical ownership while opening up new ways for gold to be used in modern financial markets,” World Gold Council CEO David Tait said in the release. “This kind of significant progress can only be achieved when the industry works together.” The pilot comes as the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority considers industry feedback on the use of tokenized gold in wholesale markets, including as collateral. The parallel developments could strengthen London’s position in the modernization of global gold-market infrastructure. The Council’s Wholesale Digital Gold initiative remains at the pilot stage and is designed to complement rather than replace existing allocated and unallocated gold settlement systems. The model allows wholesale market participants to electronically buy, sell and transfer ownership interests in a pool of segregated physical gold bars without moving the underlying metal. During the pilot, participants placed 400-oz. London Good Delivery gold bars into the system and created PGIs that granted them proprietary interests in the pooled bullion. They withdrew the metal after settling the transactions, completing the full settlement lifecycle. “Gold ownership that is fractional, readily transferable and insolvency remote would allow gold to be used more widely across financial markets, including as collateral,” J.P. Morgan global head of physical commodities Mark Amlin said. StoneX global head of metals Michael Skinner said the initiative could give clients greater flexibility, reduce operational friction and improve capital efficiency. Scaling the system will require reliable governance, technology and data management, according to IBA president Clive de Ruig, while Baton Systems CEO Arjun Jayaram highlighted the need for real-time processing and distinct data permissions for each participant. The Council first outlined the initiative in a September 2025 white paper developed with advice from Linklaters and Hilltop Walk Consulting. It continues to seek input from market participants, regulators and technology providers as it develops the framework.

title: Osisko outlines 7.4B lb. of copper underground at Gaspé
summary: Underground deposit at the Gaspé project in Quebec holds nearly double the open-pit resources grade.
body: Underground deposit at the Gaspé project in Quebec holds nearly double the open-pit resources grade. Aerial view of the Gaspé Copper project area. Credit: Osisko Metals. Osisko Metals (TSX: OM; US-OTC: OMZNF) has outlined an underground deposit containing 7.4 billion lb. of copper at its Gaspé project in eastern Quebec — at nearly twice the grade of its measured and indicated open-pit resources. The first underground estimate for Porphyry Mountain, 1.1 km northeast of the centre of the old Copper Mountain pit, puts inferred resources at 706 million tonnes grading 0.48% copper and 0.055% molybdenum, Osisko said Monday in a resource update released after markets closed. The estimate, effective Oct. 30, draws on drilling from 1994 to 2019 and new assays of some of the old core. “The size of the underground resource is larger than we anticipated,” National Bank Financial mining analyst Rabi Nizami said Tuesday in a note. Nizami had expected about 4 billion lb. of copper-equivalent metal underground, including byproducts. The open pit remains the focus of development for the next several years, he said. Osisko is working to reopen the former Noranda mine at Murdochville, about 825 km northeast of Montreal. The company modelled the deeper deposit for block caving, which uses gravity to draw broken rock into tunnels below. The company has yet to demonstrate the economics of mining it. Measured and indicated resources in the pit now total 2.15 billion tonnes grading 0.25% copper for 11.6 billion lb. of the metal. In April, the estimate stood at 1.83 billion tonnes of 0.27% copper for 10.8 billion lb. of contained metal. Osisko lowered the reporting cut-off to 0.12% copper-equivalent from 0.16%, bringing more lower-grade material into the pit estimate. A further inferred 265 million tonnes at 0.38% copper contain 2.2 billion lb. in the pit. Results from this year’s 70,000-metre drill program are due to feed into the next resource update, which is planned for April. The company expects the drilling “will significantly extend the open-pit resource to the south and southwest towards Needle Mountain,” CEO Robert Wares said. Osisko shares closed Monday at C$1.12 in Toronto before the release, valuing the company at about C$1 billion ($700 million). The shares have traded between C44.5¢ and C$1.99 over the past year.

title: Trafigura takes control of $260 million copper-gold project in Chile
summary: The commodities giant moves into mine development in the Atacama, but an Indigenous legal challenge threatens construction plans.
body: The commodities giant moves into mine development in the Atacama, but an Indigenous legal challenge threatens construction plans. Trafigura, one of the world’s largest commodities traders, has acquired full ownership of the $260-million La Farola copper-gold project in Chile, expanding beyond concentrate trading into mine development as a legal challenge threatens construction plans. The company completed on Monday its purchase of the remaining 50% of Minera Altair, the project’s owner, after holding an equal stake since 2021. Trafigura disclosed the planned acquisition in its half-year financial report for the six months ended March 2026. The purchase price was not disclosed. The deal gives Trafigura direct control over a potential source of copper concentrate rather than relying solely on supply agreements with third-party producers. It also exposes the trader to the permitting, construction and operating risks associated with developing a mine. La Farola, near Tierra Amarilla in the Atacama region, is a previously mined deposit that Altair has sought to restart since 2023. The environmentally approved project is designed to produce 90,000 tonnes of gold-bearing copper concentrate annually over a 15-year mine life. Detailed engineering began in May 2025, with construction scheduled for June 2027. That timetable, however, faces uncertainty following a legal challenge to the project’s environmental approval. In April 2026, Chile’s First Environmental Court admitted a claim filed by the Colla Tata Inti Indigenous Community of Los Loros against the Atacama Environmental Evaluation Commission’s approval decision. The community’s representatives argue that the open-pit project would affect local communities and air quality. The court heard arguments in July and subsequently took the case under review. It has yet to issue a ruling, leaving a key regulatory question unresolved ahead of Trafigura’s planned construction start. The outcome could determine whether the company can proceed on schedule or must reconsider its development plans. Despite its relatively modest scale, La Farola marks a significant step for Trafigura, which reported revenue of $141.9 billion and net profit of $4.1 billion in the first half of fiscal 2026. The project signals the company’s move toward securing copper supplies through direct ownership as competition for the metal intensifies. In August, Trafigura signed a long-term offtake agreement with Copper Giant (TSX-V: CGNT) covering 20% of the copper concentrate and 20% of the molybdenum concentrate expected from the Mocoa project in Colombia once commercial production begins. The trader linked that agreement to its strategy of bringing new supplies to a strategic minerals market facing strong demand and constrained availability. Unlike the Mocoa arrangement, which gives Trafigura rights to purchase future production, La Farola places responsibility for mine development and operations directly with the company. The acquisition also strengthens Trafigura’s growing presence in Chile, where it has traded copper for years while expanding into energy and critical minerals. In July, Trafigura and Generadora Metropolitana, one of Chile’s main electricity producers, completed the acquisition of the 273-MW Los Guindos power plant in the Biobío region. Three months later, the trader signed an agreement with EnergyX to purchase 100,000 tonnes of lithium products over 10 years in a deal valued at more than $2 billion. The contract covers 66% of planned first-phase production from EnergyX’s Black Giant project in the Antofagasta region. These investments extend Trafigura’s involvement in Chile beyond conventional commodities trading, adding exposure to electricity generation, lithium supply and copper production.

summary: The Conference Board survey released Tuesday showed improvement across the board, with the headline confidence index jumping to 103.3.
body: Consumers grew significantly more optimistic in November in the wake of the midterm elections , with a growing number of Americans now seeing improvement in the labor market and expecting inflation to cool. The Conference Board survey released Tuesday showed improvement across the board, with the headline confidence index jumping to 103.3, up 11.4 points from October and much better than the Dow Jones consensus forecast for 92.2. Confidence among Democrats and independent voters improved sharply, the Conference Board said, while confidence among Republican respondents fell slightly. Still, confidence among Republicans remained the highest among the three groups. While respondents "continued to express frustration with high prices and rising costs," they also "cited hope for the general economy," said Fergus McCormick, the board's senior economist for global indicators. The survey comes with the Federal Reserve continuing to try to bring down inflation, which has run above the central bank's 2% target for some 5½ years. The Fed is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point when it meets again in two weeks. Despite the lingering worries about the cost of living — a centerpiece issue during the midterms — the survey's present situation and expectations indexes both posted strong gains. Inflation expectations for 12 months from now fell for the second straight month but remained high at 5.7%. The survey's closely watched gap between jobs considered "plentiful" versus "hard to get" widened to 12.4 percentage points. The "plentiful" side rose to 30.8% from 26.2% while "hard to get" fell to 18.4%, down 3 percentage points. The survey results are the second in the past week to reveal that Americans are growing more optimistic about the economy. The University of Michigan's November survey, released Friday, showed a 7.3% increase since October, with a similar partisan split.

body: Markets saw a pretty significant bounce during the session yesterday, but Tuesday has seen a bit of selling pressure as the market approached the $3,700 level. The Monday bounce did look a bit dramatic on the screen, but the useful question is: what drove it? Futures on the COMEX rose nearly 4% to $3,655 after the previous sessionâs 14-month closing low, according to CME Groupâs November 23 market recap . CME linked the move to firmer equities and a change in the marketâs artificial intelligence and semiconductor narrative, including, most notably, news around NVIDIA. That is a different kind of support from fresh bullion demand. It suggests gold was recovering as cross-market risk appetite improved after the metal had been caught in the preceding weekâs broad reduction in risk appetite and overall exposure. That being said, the rebound has a clear hurdle. The CME said gold had fallen 9% over the previous week, its largest percentage decline in 8 months, and remained well below its opening level for that week, even after Mondayâs massive jump. The speed of the bounce matters, but it doesnât necessarily erase the drawdown. Buyers now need to show that they will keep adding exposure when equity impulse fades, rather than simply lifting gold during a short-lived rotation across markets. The latest regional fund-flow snapshot offers a way to test that question. The World Gold Councilâs November 23 weekly monitor , using data through November 20, shows physical-backed gold ETFs lost about 20.4 tonnes in the week. North America shed 11.8 tonnes, Europe 6.4 tonnes, and Asia 2.2 tonnes. For November 1 through 20, the regional totals were North America minus 7 tonnes, Europe minus 16 tonnes, and Asia minus 5 tonnes. The pattern changed within the month. Europe had been the largest source of November outflows overall, while North America led selling in the last week. This chart below isolates that shift. The flows are meaningful, but they donât necessarily establish a wholesale exit from gold funds. The weekly decline was concentrated in North America, while the year-to-date and longer-term ETF picture is not captured by this short window. The Councilâs ETF data page says its data set covers more than 100 physical-backed products and is updated weekly on the following Monday, with monthly downloadable detail published separately. The distinction keeps the present move in perspective. If gold rises while ETF flows continue to drain, the market may be seeing short covering or cross-asset relief rather than a renewed investment bid. If inflows return and prices hold after equities tumble, the recovery could have a bit more in the way of confirmation working for it. Neither condition is established by Mondayâs price action alone. Every new Gold analysis as it publishes, today's technical signal and key levels, live price â on one page. The CME also noted that silver and copper rose with gold, consistent with broad improvement in sentiment across metals rather than something isolated in the gold market itself. The next scheduled macro test for gold will be Wednesdayâs U.S. October personal income and outlays release, which includes the Federal Reserveâs well-followed PCE inflation measures. The Bureau of Economic Analysis calendar lists a report for 8:30 a.m. ET, and it is going to be the main event on Wednesday. The release can reset expectations for rates and inflation, but the immediate gold question is going to be how price responds. A stronger-than-expected inflation reading could pressure gold if investors think financial conditions will remain restrictive, while a cooler print could support prices if it eases that concern. That being said, itâs probably worth noting that most traders expect a 25-basis-point increase next month out of the Federal Reserve. body: Gold prices are pulling back in early Tuesday trading after Mondayâs sharp rebound from a more than one-year low, with traders questioning whether the bounce was anything more than bargain hunting after last weekâs 9% collapse. The rally on Monday had no strong fundamental catalyst behind it. Prices had simply gotten cheap enough to attract buyers after the worst weekly decline in over a year. The surprise surge in equities may have helped by lifting sentiment across risk assets, giving gold room to breathe. However, there was no shift in the rate outlook, and no change in the dollarâs strength that would justify a sustained move higher. The U.S. Dollar Index is one reason to be skeptical about the bounce. DXY is currently hovering near a 20-month high. Technically, The main trend is up according to the weekly swing chart. The index has formed a series of higher bottoms at 97.625, 98.557 and 101.099. The main range is 110.176 to 95.551. Its retracement zone is 102.864 to 104.589. DXY is trading inside this zone after recovering the 50% level at 102.864. The index is also trading above the 52-week moving average at 99.817. This is potential support. Until the Dollar Index trend turns down, itâs going to be hard for gold to gain much upside momentum. That lack of conviction on goldâs side is showing up early Tuesday as the market turns its attention to Wednesdayâs Personal Consumption Expenditures index . The PCE is the Fedâs preferred inflation gauge. Itâs also the last major data point before the December 8-9 meeting. The rate picture remains the dominant headwind. CMEâs FedWatch Tool shows traders pricing in a 97.8% probability of a 25 basis point hike in December, with the chance of a larger 50 basis point increase at 2.2%. Higher rates raise the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion, and that math has not changed. The risk now is straightforward. A hot PCE print would reinforce the Fedâs tightening path, further support the dollarâs uptrend, and could push gold to new lows below $3,500 per ounce. A softer reading would give bulls something to work with, but even then, the broader trend remains unfriendly as long as rates keep climbing and DXY holds above 102.864. Mondayâs bounce looks like a dead cat bounce until proven otherwise. The next two sessions will go a long way toward determining whether gold has found a floor or is just pausing before the next leg lower. body: Spot gold (XAU/USD) is trading near $3,620 in Tuesday’s Asian session, November 24, down about 0.4% after failing again near $3,651. Gold jumped about 3% on Monday as stocks rebounded sharply, a sign last week’s forced selling is easing. The level that matters is $3,593, with October PCE inflation, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, due on Wednesday. Spot gold rose as much as 3.5% to $3,654.97 on Monday, Reuters reported, and was near $3,635.10 in late trading, up 2.75%. US gold futures gained 4% to $3,653.70, and silver jumped 4.62% to $43.02. I flagged the start of this move in Monday morning’s forecast . Wall Street staged a huge recovery at the same time. The S&P 500 rose 4.74% to 7,237, the Nasdaq jumped 6.51% and the Dow gained 3.01%, as confidence in AI stocks returned after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive. S&P 500 since August, data through November 20, showing the slide into correction before Monday’s 4.7% rebound. Last week, investors sold gold to raise cash and meet margin calls, demands from brokers to add money when losses grow, as stocks crashed. Monday’s simultaneous rebound in equities and bullion suggests liquidation pressure is easing, though it does not confirm the broader correction is over. For me, this is the most useful signal of the week. It supports the view that last week’s 9% drop came mostly from forced selling, not from a collapse in gold’s longer-term story. Still, Goldman Sachs analysts told Reuters that the downward pressure could reverse “more slowly” around year-end, as some hedge funds may hold off on rebuilding risk. November’s flash PMIs, early surveys of business activity where readings above 50 mean growth, all slowed. The composite index fell to 54.6 from 55.9, services eased to 54.7 from 56.1, and manufacturing slipped to 54.5 from 54.9. Traders trimmed some bets on a December hike after the softer data and last week’s drop in consumers’ inflation expectations. The 10-year Treasury yield finished near 4.92% after briefly rising above 5%. Oil also kept sliding, with WTI down 3.9% at $80.17 and Brent down 3.5% at $89.37, as Middle East flows recovered and a Libyan pipeline restarted. Cheaper oil should ease inflation over time, which would give the Fed room to slow down. Natixis analyst Bernard Dahdah warned gold could fall to $3,340 by January. He pointed to a dollar that has risen about 2% since the midterms and slowing central bank buying. Poland’s central bank has reached its 700-tonne gold target, and Kazakhstan plans to cut gold’s share of its reserves to 75% from 78% by year-end, which could mean selling about 52 tonnes. “The general market sentiment is that most of the accumulation is behind us,” Dahdah said. His stress test assumes central bank demand falls 25% from 2025 levels and gold ETFs, funds that hold physical gold for investors, lose 20 tonnes a month. Britannia Bullion’s Matthew Jones takes a calmer view, expecting gold to consolidate into 2027, but warned that a sustained break below $3,500 would signal a weaker long-term structure. A soft PCE reading would ease hike bets and could help gold break the $3,651 cap, while a hot reading would put Natixis’ $3,340 target back in play. body: Selling pressure pushes Silver (XAG/USD) into negative territory during Tuesday’s European session, wiping out its initial advance. At the time of writing, the metal has fallen 1.58% to around $42.45, having pulled back from the session high of $44.00. Apparent flows of global capital back into Artificial Intelligence (AI) stocks are weighing on the white metal after Nvidia announced the reinstatement of Jense Huang as CEO. The decision marks an unexpected reversal: following confirmation of his extra-marital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, the board had explicitly ruled out his return. The exceptional corporate developments and market moves surrounding Nvidia are in focus for analysts at Danske Bank. They note that, in the US, the company “reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, less than a week after the board had ruled out his return.” According to the board, input had come from “senior levels” of the US government, and it identified no national security risk. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said he had personally persuaded the board. Calling the market response a “stunning reversal”, Danske Bank says Nvidia shares climbed “31.5% higher”, helping broader indices advance. The S&P 500 gained “4.7%” and the Nasdaq rose “6.9%.” However, the analysts warn that Nvidia “still faces SEC and Justice Department investigations over issues ranging from potential accounting irregularities to alleged chip smuggling,” while senior Democrats “have also pledged to investigate the matter once they take control of Congress in January.” Regional markets have responded differently to the initial rally, according to the bank. It observes that “the AI trade is carrying through to Asia this morning,” citing “Taiwan up 9% and South Korea up 7% at the time of writing.” Elsewhere, however, “European equity futures are flat, and US futures point to a slightly higher open,” highlighting the divergence in the immediate follow-through. The breadth of the US advance also draws scrutiny from Danske Bank, whose analysts “take issue with calling yesterday a broad rally.” Their assessment is that “US tech rose 9%, while energy and consumer staples both fell,” and that “gaps of around 10 percentage points between sectors are rare and not broad rally in our opinion.” They characterise “yesterday’s move” as “a partial reversal of the AI sell-off over the past month,” rather than a broad-based advance. Volatility remains elevated despite a decline, with the analysts noting that “the VIX fell from 36 to 26.” Additional pressure on Silver comes from a strengthening US Dollar (USD), supported by increased inflows into US equities and expectations of a hawkish Federal Reserve (Fed). A firmer Dollar makes Silver less attractive to investors from a risk-reward perspective. title: BofA favors copper and uranium, downgrades Pan American Silver - TradingView
body: BofA Securities remains positive on the medium-term outlook for copper and uranium but sees near-term risks for precious metals, according to a Nov. 24 report led by analyst Lawson Winder. The bank lowered most mining-stock price targets to reflect revised commodity forecasts and lower valuation multiples, while downgrading Pan American Silver PAAS to Neutral from Buy. Copper ( HG1:COM ) remains a preferred investment theme despite a weaker near-term price forecast. BofA cut its 2027 copper forecast by 4.1% to $6.63 a pound but expects prices to reach $7.26 a pound by the fourth quarter of that year. Tight mine supply and a rebound in Chinese demand should support prices in the second half of 2027, the bank said. Freeport-McMoRan FCX remains its top copper pick, supported by an ongoing operational turnaround and potential growth opportunities. BofA also maintained its favorable longer-term uranium outlook, citing growing nuclear demand and disciplined mine supply. It lowered its 2027 uranium ( UXA:COM ) forecast by 18.1% to $106.25 a pound while raising its 2028 estimate by 10.2% to $123.13. Cameco CCJ remains the bank’s preferred nuclear-fuel stock because of its exposure to fuel, reactor technology and services, although its price target fell to $112 from $133. BofA also cut its target for Neutral-rated Centrus Energy LEU to $100 from $147. For gold and silver, the bank expects further near-term pressure until risks of escalation in the Iran war subside and the U.S. interest-rate hiking cycle ends. It reduced its 2027 gold forecast by 7.8% to $4,438 an ounce and its silver forecast by 11.1% to $61.88, while retaining a constructive longer-term view. Precious-metals stock price targets fell by an average of 12%, and Agnico Eagle Mines AEM remains its top pick. Pan American Silver’s downgrade reflects low expected production growth in 2027, a low free-cash-flow yield and a premium valuation relative to peers, according to the report. BofA lowered its price target to $35 from $42, underscoring its more cautious stance toward precious-metals equities. Steel offered a brighter near-term pricing outlook. BofA raised its 2027 U.S. hot-rolled coil ( HRC:COM ) forecast by 33.4% to $1,300 per short ton, expecting market tightness to persist through the first quarter. Higher domestic mill utilization, new capacity and recovering imports could push the market into surplus in the second half of 2027, however. The bank retained its steel-stock ratings but lowered price targets by an average of 8%, favoring Commercial Metals CMC and Nucor NUE . title: Voltas to Blue Star: Why 15 AC, EV stocks are in focus as copper slides to 7-month low - The Financial Express
body: The sharp fall in prices of copper to a seven-month low has boosted sentiment across sectors. Copper is a key raw material, and lower prices of the red metal are expected to benefit companies across sectors, including consumer durables and automotives. A drop in copper price will primarily benefit companies that purchase copper as a raw material and are unable to fully pass the cost to consumers, or that sell at fixed prices. However, copper producers and those holding high-cost inventories remain exposed to plunging prices, according to analysts. A stronger dollar and expectations of rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve have weighed on copper. Speculative funds have been net sellers of COMEX copper futures for seven consecutive weeks. The red metal is used in air conditioning coils, compressors, motors, fans, and appliances. These companies have limited pricing power and frequently absorb cost increases, and lower copper prices will directly boost their gross margins. According to Netra Deshpande, Research Analyst at Mirae Asset Sharekhan, consumer durables and air conditioning companies will be the biggest beneficiaries of lower copper prices. Some companies which stand to benefit the most are Voltas , Blue Star , Amber Enterprises, Crompton Greaves Consumer, Havells India , and Whirlpool India, Deshpande said. Power equipment and transformer manufacturers are likely to benefit from lower prices. “Transformers use a lot of copper in their windings, and many orders are fixed-price or have limited price variation clauses. Cheaper copper improves margins on the order book being executed and alleviates the input bottleneck mentioned earlier,” she said. Transformers & Rectifiers (India) , Voltamp Transformers, Hitachi Energy India , GE Vernova T&D India , and Siemens are likely to be the main beneficiaries. Moreover, original equipment manufacturers such as Mahindra & Mahindra , Maruti Suzuki India , and Tata Motors will also benefit from lower copper prices. “EV motors, wiring harnesses, charging equipment, and grid or EPC contractors working on fixed-price projects receive cost savings,” Deshpande said. Arun Kailasan, Research Analyst at Geojit Investments also said AC makers like Voltas, Blue Star, and LG Electronics India will be the biggest beneficiaries. These companies raised prices several times this year, yet their margins stayed under pressure, so cheaper copper ahead of the summer should help them recover. “Fan and appliance makers like Crompton and Havells, and transformer and electrical equipment makers, will also benefit, though many equipment contracts pass metal price changes on to clients. The impact on automakers is moderate, as copper is a small part of their costs. Gains will show with a lag, as companies first use up stock bought at higher prices,” Kailasan said. Copper is the most expensive item for wire and cable players . However, these companies largely pass on the price effects to the end consumers. Lower copper prices can boost volumes, especially for housing wires, and reduce working capital requirements. “In the short term, however, revenue declines, and companies may incur inventory losses on lower realisations. This include Polycab, KEI Industries, RR Kabel, Finolex Cables, and Havells,” Deshpande said. Cable makers like Polycab , KEI , and Finolex Cables face a near-term hit. They hold stock bought at higher prices, so price cuts could lead to inventory losses, and dealers are likely to delay purchases, Kailasan said. “This is temporary, as lower copper prices should boost demand over time,” he added. Copper producers and companies holding high-cost inventory could face inventory valuation losses, while lower realisations may pressure earnings, according to Jateen Trivedi, VP Research Analyst – Commodity and Currency, LKP Securities. body: The latest U.S. petroleum balance shows a meaningful near-term argument against the tighter global narrative. Commercial crude stocks increased in the week ending November 13. The Energy Information Administrationâs report released on November 18 put commercial inventories at 417.8 million barrels, up 3.4 million from the prior week and 6.4 million below the same week a year earlier. This rise followed a prior draw and leaves stocks close to the same level as they were last year, rather than signaling a severe domestic shortage. Supply remains abundant. The EIA estimated U.S. crude production at 14.032 million barrels per day for the week, a 19,000-barrel-per-day increase from the previous week. The 4-week average was 14.01 million barrels per day, 1.9% above the comparable period a year earlier. Production levels like this give the domestic market a substantial buffer against demand unless, of course, refinery demand, exports, or an outage absorbs more barrels. Stable-to-rising output can help replenish stocks that were worn down a couple of weeks ago from the hurricane and, of course, exports. The situation in the WTI market is therefore less about a single weekly build and more about the direction of the domestic balance in America. A 3.4-million-barrel build is large enough to challenge a bullish inventory story, but this is only one weekly observation and can also be influenced by shipping, timing, imports, exports, and refinery runs. The EIA balance sheet is also inclusive of products and strategic stocks. Commercial crude is the relevant measure for immediate refinery market availability. The Strategic Petroleum Reserve declined by 3.2 million barrels to 276.4 million during the same week, but it is government inventory. It is not the same thing as freely available commercial supply. The fundamental balance is somewhat mixed, with the domestic inventory build and high production limiting upside unless the next release shows a reversal. The bearish reading weakens if inventories draw while refinery activity or exports absorb supply. A fresh disruption, another weather-related production loss, or a substantial pickup in product demand would also challenge the comfortable supply interpretation. title: OPEC+ at a Crossroads - Rigzone
body: The OPEC+ group is at a crossroads for 2027, analysts at BMI outlined in a report sent to Rigzone by the Fitch Group recently. In this report, the BMI analysts projected four OPEC+ production scenarios for next year, with varying degrees of probability. The scenario the analysts at BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions, saw as having the highest probability, at 45 percent, was an “uneven intervention”, in which the group conjures up “limited cuts” with “uneven participation and compliance”. BMI’s report outlined that the scenario with the second highest probability, at 25 percent, was an “effective intervention”, in which the OPEC+ policy response is “substantial”, with “broadly supported cuts” and “strong compliance”. Another scenario given a 20 percent probability in the report was “policy paralysis”, which would offer “no effective collective restraint” and another scenario given a 10 percent probability was dubbed a “market share strategy”, in which the OPEC+ policy response would amount to a “deliberate or competitively driven production expansion”. “Our central scenario sees OPEC+ attempt to defend prices but struggle to secure sufficiently broad participation or consistent compliance,” the BMI analysts said in the report. “With relatively few members capable of delivering meaningful cuts, the burden of restraint again falls disproportionately on Saudi Arabia, which provides some, albeit limited, support to the market,” they added. “The UAE’s production remains elevated, doing little to either bolster or counteract OPEC+ policy. A sizeable surplus emerges in the second half of the year, consistent with our forecast for Brent to average $65-70 per barrel in Q4 [2027],” they continued. Looking at the “effective intervention” scenario, the BMI analysts highlighted in the report that, “under the most supportive scenario for prices, OPEC+ agrees to substantial production cuts, backed by broad participation and strong compliance”. “Saudi Arabia remains central to these efforts, but other members shoulder a meaningful share of the cuts, easing the burden on Riyadh,” they added. “The UAE also moderates production, in response to weakening market conditions,” they stated. The BMI analysts went on to note that, although a surplus still emerges in H2 2027 under this scenario, “coordinated restraint limits the scale and cushions the decline in prices”. Under the “effective intervention”, BMI analysts see Brent averaging around $70-75 per barrel in the fourth quarter of next year, the report revealed. Looking at the “market share offensive” scenario in the report, the BMI analysts described it as the most bearish price scenario, outlining that OPEC+ would shift its focus “from defending prices to rebuilding its market share, chasing higher output despite weakening market conditions”. “This could reflect a deliberate reassessment of the costs of continued production restraint, or emerge from intensifying competition between major producers, particularly Saudi Arabia and the UAE,” they added. “In the latter case, Riyadh could seek to rein in Abu Dhabi by triggering a price war, but the substantial fiscal costs involved and uncertain prospects of forcing a change in UAE policy make this highly unlikely, in our view,” they continued. “In any case, additional production would significantly add to the anticipated surplus, pushing Brent into a $50-60 per barrel range in Q4 [2027],” they warned. The BMI analysts dubbed the “policy paralysis” scenario as “a less supportive scenario”, in which OPEC+ “recognizes the need for renewed restraint but fails to agree on meaningful collective action”. “Disagreements over production quotas prevent the group from mounting an effective response. title: Brent drops to $88, WTI at $79: Why oil is sliding despite Iran’s tanker attacks - Gulf News
body: Oil prices hit 3-month low as Middle East supply rises despite Hormuz tensions Oil fell to a three-month low as Middle East flows rose, Libya’s pipeline restarted and Americas exporting bumper barrels, helping cushion ongoing attacks near the Strait of Hormuz, say industry trackers. Gulf oil flows have proved more resilient than the attacks suggest. Data from trackers indicate “record" flows, thanks in no small part to bypass routes and ship-to-ship (STS) transfers. Shipping remains exposed: attacks near Hormuz have raised insurance, rerouting and delay risks. Global oil markets are easing as more barrels flow, though the threat of disruption keeps a "floor" under prices. While November picture is expected to be "softer" and tracker data is incomplete, some oil industry trackers even go so far as to claim that “Iran has lost control of Hormuz.” Real-time AIS tracking shows vessels moving, but it does not show the full picture. Analysts point to longer “dark” transits and dark loadings, where tankers switch off transponders or use ship-to-ship transfers to obscure origin and destination. That means reported flows may understate actual volumes. The market is pricing in more supply than the visible data suggests. CNBC, citing Kpler, reported that crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz averaged nearly 11.1 million barrels per day in October, about 2% lower than September, despite at least 30 vessel attacks during the month.” Kpler: The 11.1 million bpd figure is Kpler’s estimate of average October crude exports through Hormuz. Attack count: At least 30 vessels were attacked in October, according to reporting citing maritime and industry data. Wartime record: The October attack total was described as the "highest" since the war began in late February. Late-October slowdown: Kpler data also showed Hormuz crude flows fell to 7.3 million bpd in the week ended October 28, more than 40% below the pre-war baseline. Reuters/Kpler context: Middle East crude exports reached 18.99 million bpd in October, exceeding the 18.56 million bpd average in the three months before the war. IEA context: The IEA said Gulf of Oman ship-to-ship transfers helped lift total oil flows through Hormuz by 3.7 million bpd to 10.9 million bpd. The IEA said on Sept. 18 that producers outside the Gulf have added 2.3 million bopd of supply since the war began, led by the US and Brazil. US: The EIA expects US crude output to average a record 13.9 million b/d this year. That is the biggest absolute gain of any country. Brazil: Output hit a record 4.475 million b/d in June, 19.1% above a year earlier. The EIA forecasts it adding 0.61 million b/d in 2026, the largest gain after the US. Petrobras's P-79 platform, which started on May 1, came online three months early. Guyana: Production is about 900,000 b/d from four Exxon-operated floating production vessels, up from zero in 2019. The Uaru project (250,000 b/d) targets first oil in Q4 2026. Argentina: Output reached a record 973,700 b/d in September, up 15.5% year on year, with Vaca Muerta shale supplying about 71%. Canada: The EIA forecasts +0.13 million b/d in 2026. The Trans Mountain pipeline is running close to capacity. Venezuela: It also posted first-half gains that beat prewar forecasts. Sanctions have been lifted and the hydrocarbons law overhauled. Oil's December-January timespread has collapsed from $3.67 a barrel in October to just $0.16 now. Backwardation has all but vanished, too. Backwardation means near-term barrels cost more than later barrels, usually a sign of tight supply. The move toward " contango " means later barrels are becoming more expensive than near-term ones, signalling expectations of looser supply ahead. Expectations of a global supply surplus and a larger than expected build in US stockpiles drove the decline. The crude oil price today is steady because two forces are balancing each other. Crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels, adding to supply. Goldman Sachs expects oversupply to last until 2027. title: Why India is buying less Russian oil despite Moscow offering bigger discounts - The Financial Express
body: For almost four years, Russian crude remained a major part of India’s oil imports, largely because it was available at lower prices than supplies from other countries. Even as Western sanctions disrupted trade and tensions in the Middle East threatened supplies, Russian oil continued to reach Indian ports at attractive discounts. But that advantage is now weakening. Indian refiners are progressively turning to cheaper supplies from the Middle East, Brazil and West Africa, putting pressure on Russian oil sellers to lower their prices further. Discounts on Russian Urals crude at Indian ports have widened as competition from other suppliers has reduced demand, three traders told Reuters. Cargoes scheduled for delivery in late December and January are now being offered at $2-$3 per barrel below Dated Brent on a delivered basis. Just a few weeks ago, the discount was around $1-$2 per barrel. Russian sellers are already dealing with thin margins because of high shipping costs, delays in exports and weaker global oil prices. The arrival of more cargoes from West Africa and the Middle East has added to the pressure, forcing Russian suppliers to offer bigger discounts to attract Indian buyers. While a discount of $2-3 per barrel may not appear significant, the change points to a bigger shift in India’s oil market. The cheap Russian oil that Indian refiners relied on since 2022 is facing competition from suppliers that are now offering better prices and easier shipping routes. The shift began after the US imposed sanctions on Russian oil companies Rosneft and Lukoil in late 2025. Indian refiners cut their purchases, bringing Russian oil arrivals down to around 1.2 million barrels per day (bpd) in December 2025 from 1.84 million bpd in November, according to Kpler. This was the lowest level since December 2022. The pressure continued in January, with February-loading Urals cargoes trading at nearly $10 per barrel below dated Brent at Indian ports, close to the biggest discount recorded at the time, according to traders cited by Reuters. However, the Iran war changed the picture. As supplies from the Middle East became uncertain, Indian refiners began buying Russian oil floating near the country’s coast in early March. India has crude stocks to meet only around 25 days of demand. Kpler analyst Sumit Ritolia had said refiners could quickly turn back to Russian crude if Gulf supplies came under pressure. India’s shipments through the Strait of Hormuz fell from an average of 2.8 million bpd in February to just 247,000 bpd in April. With Gulf supplies disrupted, Russian crude became a key alternative. Urals even traded at a premium to Brent at Indian ports within a week of the war starting, the first time this had happened, according to traders. Russia’s share of India’s crude imports fell to around 35% in September from as much as 56% in July, as Middle Eastern supplies recovered and Russian oil became less competitive on price. Brent prices jumped to 120-135 per barrel in October due to physical shortages in Northern Europe. Russian sellers were slow to adjust their prices, making Urals more expensive than competing grades. By November, Gulf supplies had overtaken Russian shipments for the first time since the Iran war began. Kpler data cited by Bloomberg showed that oil arriving in India through the Strait of Hormuz rose to 2.1 million barrels per day (bpd), compared with Russian imports of around 1.8 million bpd. The recovery has been supported by increased tanker movements through Hormuz, while Middle Eastern sellers are offering competitive prices. Higher freight costs and longer shipping routes have made Russian crude less attractive. Middle Eastern supplies to India stood at around 2.3 million bpd in October, when the country’s total crude imports reached a record 5.6 million bpd.
